questions.explain: The piston raises bellows pressure ahead of the real static pressure change.

cards.question: To which two subgroups can every instrument of the classical cockpit be assigned
options: Airframe monitoring and aircraft monitoring
Flight monitoring and aircraft monitoring
Flight monitoring and engine monitoring
cards.explain: The text splits classical cockpit instruments into flight monitoring and aircraft monitoring.

cards.question: To which group does the artificial horizon indicator ADI belong
options: Aircraft monitoring
Flight monitoring
Airframe monitoring
cards.explain: The ADI is listed among the flight monitoring instruments.

cards.question: Which group of instruments does the standby set of a modern cockpit duplicate
options: engine monitoring
airframe monitoring
flight monitoring
cards.explain: Altimeter, airspeed indicator, horizon and compass are all listed as flight monitoring instruments.

cards.question: An exhaust gas temperature indicator is fitted in a classical cockpit. Which group and subdivision does it belong to?
options: Aircraft monitoring, as an engine monitoring device
Aircraft monitoring, as an airframe monitoring device
Flight monitoring, as a pressure monitoring device
cards.explain: Exhaust gas temperature indicators are named as engine monitoring devices under aircraft monitoring.

cards.question: Into which two kinds of devices is aircraft monitoring divided
options: Airframe monitoring devices and standby devices
Flight monitoring devices and engine monitoring devices
Airframe monitoring devices and engine monitoring devices
cards.explain: Aircraft monitoring covers airframe monitoring devices and engine monitoring devices.

cards.question: Why do the aircraft monitoring systems of the modern cockpit carry different names such as EICAS or ECAM
options: Because the name depends on the display size
Because the name depends on the flight phase
Because the name depends on the aircraft type
cards.explain: The text states that aircraft monitoring instruments have different names depending on aircraft type.

cards.question: Which task do EICAS and ECAM perform in the modern cockpit
options: They perform flight monitoring
They perform aircraft monitoring
They perform maintenance data recording
cards.explain: EICAS and ECAM are the names given to the aircraft monitoring instruments.

cards.question: Why is the CMS counted as part of aircraft monitoring
options: Because it delivers information to the standby instruments
Because it delivers information to the maintenance personnel
Because it delivers information to the flight crew
cards.explain: The CMS is used for aircraft monitoring because it delivers information to maintenance personnel.

cards.question: The electronic displays of a glass cockpit are lost in flight. Which speed and attitude information remains available from the standby set?
options: Airspeed from the standby airspeed indicator and heading from the standby horizon
Mach number from the standby machmeter and attitude from the standby horizon
Airspeed from the standby airspeed indicator and attitude from the standby horizon
cards.explain: The standby set contains an airspeed indicator and a horizon, but no machmeter.

cards.question: A fuel pressure indication changes during flight. Which value is the instrument responding to?
options: Pressure of fluids
Earth's magnetism
Pressure of air
cards.explain: Fluid pressure is listed separately from air pressure as a value that operates instruments.

cards.question: An aircraft presents its altimeter, airspeed indicator and artificial horizon indicator on electronic displays. To which system of the modern cockpit are these instruments assigned?
options: CMS (Central Maintenance System)
EICAS (Engine Indicating and Crew Alerting System)
EFIS (Electronic Flight Instrument System)
cards.explain: All three named instruments are listed as flight monitoring instruments, and flight monitoring instruments go to the EFIS.

cards.question: The standby devices of a modern cockpit cover all but one of the flight parameters shown on the PFD. Which parameter is left without a standby device
options: altitude
vertical speed
airspeed
cards.explain: The standby set holds altimeter, airspeed indicator, horizon and compass, so of the PFD parameters only vertical speed has no standby device.

cards.question: An engineer needs aircraft system information for troubleshooting rather than an indication meant for the crew. Which aircraft monitoring system delivers it?
options: The EFIS (Electronic Flight Instrument System)
The ECAM (Electronic Centralized Aircraft Monitoring)
The CMS (Central Maintenance System)
cards.explain: The CMS is the aircraft monitoring system that delivers information to the maintenance personnel.

cards.question: A panel layout is described as Basic T. Which four instruments form that T?
options: Airspeed indicator, attitude indicator, altimeter and compass
Attitude indicator, altimeter, compass and turn coordinator
Airspeed indicator, attitude indicator, altimeter and vertical speed indicator
cards.explain: The four instruments arranged in the T shape are the airspeed indicator, attitude indicator, altimeter and compass; turn coordination and vertical speed sit below them.

cards.question: Where is the attitude indicator located in the Basic T configuration
options: In the middle at the top
In the middle at the bottom
On the left at the top
cards.explain: The Basic T places the attitude indicator centrally at the top of the group.

cards.question: Of the two combined indicators, which one adds the flight director indication and which one adds radio navigation indications
options: the ADI and the magnetic standby compass respectively
the HSI and the ADI respectively
the ADI and the HSI respectively
cards.explain: The ADI adds the flight director indication to the artificial horizon; the HSI adds radio navigation indications to the compass.

cards.question: A pilot reads his magnetic heading and a VOR course deviation from one round instrument. Which indicator is he using?
options: The ADI
The variometer
The HSI
cards.explain: The HSI is the instrument that combines compass and radio navigation information.

cards.question: A glass cockpit aircraft has no separate round flight instruments. Which statement describes the arrangement of the flight parameters?
options: They are laid out on the PFD and correspond to the Basic T configuration
They are laid out on the PFD in a configuration that replaces the Basic T
They are laid out on the navigation display in Basic T configuration
cards.explain: The PFD keeps the Basic T arrangement rather than abandoning it.

cards.question: An instrument is to be fitted in the middle at the top of a Basic T panel and must also display the indication from the flight director system. Which indicator is required?
options: The horizontal situation indicator HSI
The attitude director indicator ADI
The turn coordination indicator
cards.explain: The middle top position of the Basic T carries the attitude indicator, and the ADI is the attitude indicator that also shows the flight director indication.

cards.question: What is the proportion of nitrogen in dry, clean air directly above the surface of the earth
cards.explain: Nitrogen makes up 78% of dry clean air at the surface.

cards.question: What is the proportion of oxygen in dry, clean air directly above the surface of the earth
cards.explain: Oxygen makes up 21% of dry clean air at the surface.

cards.question: An air data system is being described to a student. Which two measurements does flight monitoring require?
options: Static pressure and dynamic pressure
Static pressure and air density
Dynamic pressure and air temperature
cards.explain: Flight monitoring is built on the two pressures, static and dynamic.

cards.question: What is the other name for dynamic pressure
options: Ram pressure
Atmospheric pressure
Barometric pressure
cards.explain: Dynamic pressure is the ram pressure produced by the aircraft's motion.

cards.question: How does the temperature behave with increasing height in the troposphere
options: It decreases by 6.5 °C every 100 metres
It decreases by 0.65 °C every 100 metres
It increases by 0.65 °C every 100 metres
cards.explain: The troposphere lapse rate is 0.65 °C per 100 m of climb.

cards.question: Which air data measurement is also called atmospheric pressure and which one is also called ram pressure
options: the dynamic pressure and the static pressure respectively
the static pressure and the total pressure respectively
the static pressure and the dynamic pressure respectively
cards.explain: The manual gives atmospheric pressure as the other name for static pressure and ram pressure as the other name for dynamic pressure.

cards.question: Which two indications become possible once temperature is applied as a corrective value
options: true airspeed and static air temperature
barometric altitude and true airspeed
airspeed and vertical speed
cards.explain: Temperature as a corrective value makes true airspeed and static air temperature available.

cards.question: How do static pressure, temperature and density behave as altitude increases
options: All three become higher
Only temperature becomes lower
All three become lower
cards.explain: All three listed values fall with increasing altitude.

cards.question: True airspeed and static air temperature are to be indicated as well. Which value must be applied as a corrective?
options: Temperature
Density
Humidity
cards.explain: Temperature is the corrective value that makes TAS and SAT available.

cards.question: A pneumatic instrument is calibrated in the workshop. Which values form the basis of that calibration?
options: The standard atmosphere values at mean sea level
The actual airfield values at the time of installation
The tropopause values of the standard atmosphere
cards.explain: Calibration is referred to the ISA mean sea level values.

cards.question: Why has the international standard atmosphere been established
options: To predict the weather conditions along a planned route
To compare flight performance under greatly differing conditions
To set the pressure scale of the altimeter before every flight
cards.explain: The ISA exists so performance figures can be compared on a common basis.

cards.question: A crew flies at a level that lies inside the troposphere over the equator but above it over the poles. Which printed thicknesses account for this?
options: About 16.8 km at the equator and about 8.5 km at the poles
About 8.5 km at the equator and about 16.8 km at the poles
About 16.8 km at the equator and about 11 km at the poles
cards.explain: The troposphere reaches much higher at the equator than at the poles, so the same level can be inside it in one place and above it in the other.

cards.question: An aircraft climbs and its static pressure falls. Which indication does a mechanical air data instrument derive from that falling pressure
options: the barometric altitude
the static air temperature
the indicated airspeed
cards.explain: Static pressure falls as altitude increases, and it is the static pressure that a mechanical instrument uses for barometric altitude.

cards.question: An air data system has static and dynamic pressure available but no temperature input. Which indication is it unable to produce
options: the vertical speed
the barometric altitude
the true airspeed
cards.explain: Barometric altitude, vertical speed and airspeed come from the two pressures alone, while true airspeed needs temperature as a corrective value.

cards.question: An airspeed indicator with bellows works on the difference between total and static pressure. Of the two air data measurements required for flight monitoring, which one does it use for this
options: the barometric altitude
the static pressure
the dynamic pressure
cards.explain: Dynamic pressure is the difference between total and static pressure, so the bellows instrument is working on the dynamic pressure of the two measurements.

cards.question: In cruise above the transition altitude all pilots set 1013.2 hPa on the altimeter. Which standard atmosphere value is this setting taken from?
options: The pressure at the tropopause
The pressure at mean sea level
The pressure at the transition level
cards.explain: The standard atmosphere fixes the sea level pressure at 1013,25 hPa, which is the pressure the crew sets for flight levels.

cards.question: How does the air temperature of the standard atmosphere behave with increasing height directly above the tropopause
options: It begins to rise with height
It continues to fall at the same rate
It stops falling and stays constant
cards.explain: Identical temperatures at both levels show the lapse rate has stopped at the tropopause.

cards.question: What does HUD stand for
options: Head Up Display
Head Unit Display
Heading Up Display
cards.explain: HUD is short for Head Up Display.

cards.question: Where is the reference level set on the altimeter
options: On the vertical speed scale
On the altitude drum
On the pressure scale
cards.explain: The reference is entered on the altimeter's pressure scale, and the indication follows from it.

cards.question: What is elevation
options: The altitude of the aircraft above mean sea level
The altitude of an object on the ground above mean sea level
The altitude of the aircraft above the ground
cards.explain: Elevation refers to something on the ground measured from mean sea level.

cards.question: An operator prepares its fleet for RVSM operations. What does this abbreviation mean?
options: The doubling of vertical safety distances at higher flight altitudes
The halving of lateral safety distances at higher flight altitudes
The halving of vertical safety distances at higher flight altitudes
cards.explain: Reduced vertical separation minimum halves the vertical spacing used up high.

cards.question: What is RVSM airspace
options: Airspace above FL 290 with 2000 ft vertical separation
Airspace above FL 290 with 1000 ft vertical separation
Airspace above FL 285 with 500 ft vertical separation
cards.explain: RVSM airspace starts above FL 290 and uses 1000 ft spacing.

cards.question: Who must receive additional mandatory training for the introduction of RVSM
options: Maintenance personnel and ground handlers
Pilots and maintenance personnel
Pilots and air traffic controllers
cards.explain: Training covers both flight crew and maintenance staff.

cards.question: Where can the conversion from pressure to indication take place
options: In the pitot probe itself or separately in the instrument
In the instrument itself or separately in air data calculators
In the instrument itself or separately in the transponder
cards.explain: Either the instrument does the whole job or a separate air data calculator does the conversion.

cards.question: Two aircraft show the same air data but the instruments work differently inside. On what does the way they function depend?
options: On the manufacturer and the reference pressure selected
On the manufacturer and the state of technological development
On the operator and the altitude monitoring programme
cards.explain: The manual attributes the differences to manufacturer and technology level.

cards.question: In a modern indicating system, how is all the air data information presented
options: on one screen called the HUD
on separate electrical instruments
on one screen called the PFD
cards.explain: Modern indicating systems gather all the air data information onto the PFD.

cards.question: How does the HUD present the PFD data
options: So that the pilot can see it only when the autopilot is engaged
So that the pilot can see it when he looks down at the centre pedestal
So that the pilot can see it when he looks through the windshield
cards.explain: The HUD projects the PFD information into the pilot's forward view.

cards.question: Which of the two transition terms applies prior to landing
options: the transition altitude
the flight level
the transition level
cards.explain: The transition altitude belongs to the climb after take-off and the transition level to the approach prior to landing.

cards.question: A barometric altimeter is set to QFE while the aircraft stands on the airfield. What does it indicate?
options: Zero altitude
Airfield elevation
Current flight level
cards.explain: With QFE set the reading starts from the airfield, so it is zero on the ground.

cards.question: What does a barometric altimeter set to QFE indicate in flight
options: The altitude above mean sea level, as long as the air pressure does not change
The flight level, as long as the air pressure does not change
The height above the airfield, as long as the air pressure does not change
cards.explain: QFE gives height above the airfield, valid while the pressure stays as set.

cards.question: An aircraft stands on an airfield with QNH set on its altimeter. What does the altimeter show?
options: Airfield elevation
Transition level
Zero altitude
cards.explain: QNH refers the altimeter to mean sea level, so on the ground it reads the airfield elevation.

cards.question: A crew selects QNH on both altimeters. In which phases of flight is this setting used?
options: During landing and take-off, above transition altitude and above transition level
During cruise, above transition altitude and above transition level
During landing and take-off, up to transition altitude and below transition level
cards.explain: QNH belongs to the low level phases, below the transition altitude or level.

cards.question: Above which altitude do all pilots set the standard pressure in cruise flight
options: 5000 ft above mean sea level
10000 ft above mean sea level
2000 ft above mean sea level
cards.explain: The transition altitude quoted here is 5000 ft MSL.

cards.question: All aircraft in cruise use the same standard pressure setting. Which purpose does this serve?
options: It ensures correct indication of the airfield elevation
It ensures safe vertical separation
It ensures a correct height above the airfield
cards.explain: A common reference means all altimeters err alike, which keeps the vertical spacing valid.

cards.question: What is the transition altitude
options: Prior to landing, the height at which the altimeter is set from QNH to STD
After take-off, the height at which the altimeter is set from QNH to STD
After take-off, the height at which the altimeter is set from STD to QNH
cards.explain: The transition altitude is the climb-out point for changing to the standard setting.

cards.question: What is the transition level
options: Prior to landing, the last usable flight level at which the altimeter is set from STD to QNH
After take-off, the last usable flight level at which the altimeter is set from STD to QNH
Prior to landing, the last usable flight level at which the altimeter is set from QNH to STD
cards.explain: The transition level is the descent point for changing back to QNH.

cards.question: What is the purpose of reducing the vertical separation minimum
options: To reduce the workload of the air data computers
To accommodate more aircraft in the same airspace
To allow aircraft to climb above the tropopause
cards.explain: More usable levels mean more aircraft fit into the same volume of airspace.

cards.question: Why was the separation above FL 285 formerly increased
options: Lack of radar coverage and reduced transponder range at high altitude
Lack of measurement precision and reduced altimeter sensitivity at high altitude
Lack of autopilot authority and reduced control response at high altitude
cards.explain: Altimeters become less precise with height, so a bigger buffer was needed.

cards.question: Besides the pitot-static sensors, the air data computers, the altimeters and the autopilot in altitude hold mode, which further item is listed as RVSM-sensitive?
options: The transponder antenna and its surroundings
The radio altimeter antennas and their surroundings
The structure and surroundings of the pitot-static sensors
cards.explain: The list of RVSM-sensitive components closes with the structure and surroundings of the pitot-static sensors.

cards.question: What is the function of the warning device required for flight in RVSM airspace
options: It indicates when the aircraft enters RVSM airspace
It indicates when the altimeter setting differs from 1013.2 hPa
It indicates when the aircraft leaves the predetermined height
cards.explain: The device warns the crew that the selected altitude is being left.

cards.question: Which autopilot capability is required for flight in RVSM airspace
options: It must be able to maintain the heading
It must be able to maintain the airspeed
It must be able to maintain the altitude
cards.explain: RVSM depends on the autopilot holding the selected altitude accurately.

cards.question: Which transponder requirement applies to an aircraft flying in RVSM airspace?
options: It must transmit heading and be connected to the altitude measurement unit
It must transmit altitude and be connected to the altitude measurement unit
It must transmit altitude and be connected to the radio altimeter
cards.explain: The transponder must report altitude taken from the altitude measurement unit.

cards.question: Which operational advantage is gained by an RVSM approved aircraft
options: It can use the increased number of flight levels to fly above the tropopause
It can use the increased number of flight levels to save time and fuel
It can use a reduced number of flight levels to save maintenance costs
cards.explain: More available levels give better routings, saving time and fuel.

cards.question: A workshop is being prepared for the maintenance of RVSM approved aircraft. Which of the mandatory training subjects concerns the accuracy of the workshop's own equipment?
options: The configuration of air data systems
Improved precision of test equipment
Improved altimeter precision
cards.explain: Improved precision of test equipment is the listed subject that deals with the equipment used to test the aircraft.

cards.question: A fleet of six aircraft is to be cleared for RVSM. Who must apply for the Airworthiness Approval and for what?
options: The aircraft operator, for each individual aircraft
The aircraft manufacturer, for each individual aircraft
The aircraft operator, for the whole fleet at once
cards.explain: Approval is per aircraft and is applied for by the operator.

cards.question: What does the requirement for RVSM Airworthiness Approval mean for each individual aircraft
options: Modification according to required service bulletins and a full static system overhaul
Replacement of the air data computers and the altitude monitoring programme
Modification according to required service bulletins and the altitude monitoring programme
cards.explain: The manual says each aircraft must be modified per the required service bulletins and is subject to the altitude monitoring programme.

cards.question: Which detail of the air data computer must the mandatory RVSM training cover
options: Its cooling airflow
Its part numbers
Its software loading procedure
cards.explain: The training list names the part numbers of the air data computer.

cards.question: An aircraft has electrical air data instruments fed from separate air data calculators. In this fit, where does the conversion from pressure by mechanical means take place
options: in the pitot and static probes
separately from the instrument
in the instrument itself
cards.explain: Where the instruments are electrical and the calculators separate, the mechanical conversion happens in those calculators and not in the instrument.

cards.question: One screen in the cockpit carries all the air data information and also every Basic T parameter. Which screen is this
options: the PFD (Primary Flight Display)
the HUD (Head Up Display)
the standby horizon
cards.explain: The PFD is the screen that holds all the air data information, and it shows every one of the Basic T parameters.

cards.question: Two altimeters on the same parked aircraft are read at the airfield, one showing zero and the other showing the airfield elevation. Which settings are selected?
options: QFE on the first and QNE on the second
QFE on the first and QNH on the second
QNH on the first and QFE on the second
cards.explain: With QFE the barometric altimeter reads zero on the airfield, while with QNH it reads the elevation there.

cards.question: An aircraft climbs through the transition altitude after take-off. Which change of altimeter setting is required?
options: From QNH to STD (QNE)
From QFE to QNH
From STD (QNE) to QNH
cards.explain: The transition altitude is the height at which the altimeter is changed from QNH to the standard setting.

cards.question: An aircraft descends through the transition level on the approach. Which change of altimeter setting is required?
options: From QNH to QFF
From STD (QNE) to QNH
From QNH to STD (QNE)
cards.explain: The transition level is the flight level at which the altimeter is changed from the standard setting back to QNH.

cards.question: The low range radio altimeter is unserviceable and the crew needs the height above the airfield. Which setting gives it on the barometric altimeter, and under which condition?
options: QNH, in as far as there is no change in air pressure
QFE, in as far as there is no change in air pressure
QFE, in as far as the aircraft stays below the transition altitude
cards.explain: Height is normally taken from the low range radio altimeter, and the barometric altimeter on QFE gives it only as long as the air pressure does not change.

cards.question: An aircraft in cruise above the transition altitude keeps QNH set instead of the standard pressure. What is no longer ensured
options: the indication of the airfield elevation
the measurement of the height above the ground
the safe vertical separation from other aircraft
cards.explain: The common 1013.2 hPa setting in cruise is what ensures safe vertical separation, so an aircraft left on QNH no longer has it.

cards.question: An aircraft cruises at 4000 ft above mean sea level in an area with a transition altitude of 5000 ft. Which altimeter setting must be used?
options: QNE
QNH
QFF
cards.explain: Standard setting only applies above the transition altitude, so below it the altimeter stays on QNH.

cards.question: RVSM airspace lies above FL 290 and is therefore flown on flight levels. What must the altimeter be set to there
options: the standard setting of 1013.2 hPa
the QFE of the departure airfield
the QNH of the destination airfield
cards.explain: RVSM airspace is flight level airspace, and flight levels are flown with the standard pressure of 1013.2 hPa set.

cards.question: An aircraft is cleared to a level above FL 290. Which vertical separation applies there and what is the airspace called?
options: 1000 ft separation, known as MNPS airspace
1000 ft separation, known as RVSM airspace
2000 ft separation, known as RVSM airspace
cards.explain: Above FL 290 the vertical separation is 1000 ft and that airspace is called RVSM airspace.

cards.question: An aircraft has one altimeter, an autopilot that can hold the altitude, a height deviation warning and a transponder with altitude transmission. Which RVSM equipment requirement does it fail to meet
options: two independent altimeters
an autopilot for altitude hold
a transponder with altitude transmission
cards.explain: Three of the four required items are fitted, but RVSM needs two independent altimeters and the aircraft has only one.

cards.question: An autopilot can no longer hold the selected altitude. Which requirement for flight in RVSM airspace is no longer met?
options: A device for indicating when leaving the predetermined height
A transponder with altitude transmission
An autopilot that can maintain the altitude
cards.explain: One of the listed items of RVSM equipment is an autopilot able to maintain the altitude, and that is the function lost.

cards.question: A dent is found in the skin close to a static port of an RVSM approved aircraft. Which consequence must be expected?
options: A considerable influence on the altitude indication
A considerable influence on the mach number only
A considerable influence on the radio altimeter indication
cards.explain: Skin damage near the static source disturbs the static pressure and so the altitude reading.

cards.question: An altimeter fails in cruise and the aircraft loses its RVSM capability. Which action is required?
options: A change of the altimeter setting to QNH
A descent to the transition level
A quick exit of RVSM airspace
cards.explain: Losing RVSM capability means the aircraft must leave RVSM airspace quickly.

cards.question: What does the abbreviation IAS stand for
options: Inertial airspeed
Indicated airspeed
Increased airspeed
cards.explain: The text defines IAS as indicated airspeed.

cards.question: Which airspeed is displayed in aircraft equipped with air data computers and glass cockpits
options: The calibrated airspeed
The true airspeed
The equivalent airspeed
cards.explain: Glass cockpits with an ADC display CAS.

cards.question: For which purpose is the true airspeed needed
options: For engine trim purposes
For navigation purposes
For design data purposes
cards.explain: The manual states TAS is required for navigation.

cards.question: An airspeed indicator with bellows is connected to the pitot and static systems. Which pressure does its indication directly follow?
options: The static pressure as the difference between ambient and total pressure
The dynamic pressure as the difference between total and static pressure
The total pressure as the sum of dynamic and ambient pressure
cards.explain: IAS follows dynamic pressure, which is total pressure minus static pressure.

cards.question: Under which conditions does an airspeed indicator with bellows show the real speed of the aircraft
options: At cruise altitude with standard conditions
At mean sea level with compressibility corrected
At mean sea level with standard conditions
cards.explain: The bellows instrument is only true at mean sea level in standard conditions.

cards.question: An air data computer converts the indicated airspeed into the calibrated airspeed. Which two errors does it remove?
options: The error from the indicator and the error from the static pressure source
The error from the pitot source and the error from air density
The error from the indicator and the error from air compressibility
cards.explain: CAS is IAS corrected for instrument error and static source error.

cards.question: A mechanical standby airspeed indicator with bellows is fed with total and static pressure. Which airspeed does it display?
options: The equivalent airspeed
The indicated airspeed
The calibrated airspeed
cards.explain: A bellows instrument with no computer correction shows IAS.

cards.question: Of the two speeds derived after the calibrated airspeed, which one is needed for navigation and which one is kept for design data
options: the true airspeed and the indicated airspeed respectively
the equivalent airspeed and the true airspeed respectively
the true airspeed and the equivalent airspeed respectively
cards.explain: The true airspeed is the one wanted for navigation; the equivalent airspeed is not indicated and serves design data and further calculations.

cards.question: Under which condition is the speed formula valid
options: Only when the medium used is at standard temperature
Only when the medium used is above the tropopause
Only when the medium used is incompressible
cards.explain: The formula assumes an incompressible medium.

cards.question: An aircraft accelerates to a high speed and the total pressure rises more than the speed formula predicts. What produces this additional pressure?
options: Air expands at higher speeds and generates a total pressure decrease
Air compresses at lower speeds and generates a static pressure increase
Air compresses at higher speeds and generates a total pressure increase
cards.explain: Compression of the air at high speed raises the total pressure, which the instrument reads as extra speed.

cards.question: How does the compressibility error change with airspeed and altitude
options: The higher the airspeed and altitude, the larger the error
The lower the airspeed and the higher the altitude, the larger the error
The higher the airspeed and altitude, the smaller the error
cards.explain: The error grows with both airspeed and altitude.

cards.question: What is the equivalent airspeed
options: The calibrated airspeed after the compressibility error has been removed
The indicated airspeed after the instrument error has been removed
The true airspeed after the density calculation has been removed
cards.explain: EAS is what is left when the compressibility error is taken out of CAS.

cards.question: Why is the equivalent airspeed not shown to the crew of a commercial airplane
options: It is only available when the air data computer is in test
It is only valid below the tropopause in standard conditions
It is only important for design data and further calculations
cards.explain: EAS is a design and calculation value, not a cockpit indication.

cards.question: A navigation computation needs the speed of the aircraft through the surrounding air mass. Which airspeed is this?
options: The calibrated airspeed
The true airspeed
The equivalent airspeed
cards.explain: TAS is the aircraft speed relative to the surrounding air mass.

cards.question: In which order are the airspeeds derived from the pressure inputs
options: CAS, IAS, TAS, EAS
IAS, EAS, CAS, TAS
IAS, CAS, EAS, TAS
cards.explain: The summary chain runs IAS to CAS to EAS to TAS.

cards.question: Which calculation is made between EAS and TAS
options: A density calculation
A compressibility correction
A static source correction
cards.explain: The last step of the chain is the density calculation.

cards.question: A standby airspeed indicator with bellows and the airspeed readout of the glass cockpit are read at the same moment and differ. Which airspeeds are the two showing?
options: Calibrated airspeed on the bellows instrument and indicated airspeed on the glass cockpit
Indicated airspeed on the bellows instrument and true airspeed on the glass cockpit
Indicated airspeed on the bellows instrument and calibrated airspeed on the glass cockpit
cards.explain: A bellows instrument shows the indicated airspeed, while the glass cockpit indication is the calibrated airspeed.

cards.question: The indicated airspeed follows the dynamic pressure directly, and the speed formula behind it holds only for an incompressible medium. At high speed, which behaviour of the air affects the indication
options: cools and generates a static pressure increase
expands and generates a total pressure decrease
compresses and generates a total pressure increase
cards.explain: IAS depends directly on the dynamic pressure, and at higher speeds the air compresses and adds to the total pressure, which the formula does not allow for.

cards.question: Navigation needs the real speed of the aircraft measured against the surrounding air, but the cockpit shows only the airspeed indication. Which speed is needed and which value must be applied to obtain it?
options: The true airspeed, obtained by applying static pressure as a corrective value
The equivalent airspeed, obtained by applying temperature as a corrective value
The true airspeed, obtained by applying temperature as a corrective value
cards.explain: Navigation needs the true airspeed, and temperature is the corrective value applied so that the true airspeed can be indicated.

cards.question: Why is the equivalent airspeed lower than the calibrated airspeed at high speed and altitude?
options: Because compression of the air lowers the static pressure, so the indication is too low
Because reduced density lowers the total pressure, so the indication is too high
Because compression of the air raises the total pressure, so the indication is too high
cards.explain: The extra total pressure from compression makes the reading too high, so the correction reduces the speed.

cards.question: Two aircraft fly at the same calibrated airspeed, one at 20,000 ft and one at 40,000 ft. Which one has the larger compressibility error?
options: The aircraft at 40,000 ft
Both have the same error
The aircraft at 20,000 ft
cards.explain: The error grows with altitude, so the higher aircraft has the larger error.

cards.question: What forms the sensing element of an aneroid barometer
options: A small chamber made of thin glass
A small capsule made of thin metal
A small tube filled with thin fluid
cards.explain: The aneroid element is a thin metal capsule.

cards.question: What is the function of a Bourdon tube
options: It converts pressure into a proportional electrical signal
It converts pressure into a proportional temperature signal
It converts vibration into a proportional electrical signal
cards.explain: The Bourdon tube arrangement turns pressure into a proportional electrical output.

cards.question: Which cross-sectional shape does the curved tube of a Bourdon transducer have
options: An oval shape
A round shape
A square shape
cards.explain: The tube has an oval cross section in the unpressurised state.

cards.question: Which stroke do diaphragm capsules supply as the measurable value
options: 14 to 15 mm
0.4 to 0.5 mm
4 to 5 mm
cards.explain: The capsule stroke is only 4 to 5 mm.

cards.question: The aneroid barometer takes its name from a neros, not fluid. What is its sensing element
options: a curved tube with an oval cross section
a vertical tube filled with a fluid
a small capsule made of thin metal
cards.explain: An aneroid barometer senses pressure with a thin metal capsule and so needs no liquid at all.

cards.question: What creates the negative pressure at the top of a liquid barometer tube
options: The fluid flowing out of the tube due to its own weight
The expansion of the glass tube with temperature
The ambient air pressure acting on the container
cards.explain: The weight of the fluid draws it down and leaves a negative pressure above it.

cards.question: How does an aneroid capsule react to increasing air pressure
options: It is compressed
It is unchanged
It is expanded
cards.explain: Rising pressure squeezes the capsule, so it contracts.

cards.question: Which pressure is applied to the outside of the capsule in an aneroid altimeter
options: The static pressure
The dynamic pressure
The total pressure
cards.explain: The aircraft aneroid altimeter senses static pressure acting on an evacuated capsule.

cards.question: Which additional provision, beyond the pressure capsule and the indicating linkage, is built into an aneroid altimeter
options: A compensation for the effect of acceleration
A compensation for the effect of temperature
A compensation for the effect of humidity
cards.explain: The aneroid altimeter carries a temperature compensation in addition to the capsule and the indicating linkage.

cards.question: A Bourdon tube transducer is opened for inspection. Which two parts carry out the pressure conversion?
options: The straight tube and a position sensor
The curved tube and a drive coil
The curved tube and a position sensor
cards.explain: Only the curved oval tube and a position sensor at its tip are required.

cards.question: A Bourdon tube transducer is fitted with a synchro transmitter. Which quantity does this sensor convert into an electrical signal?
options: The pressure inside the tube
The temperature of the tube wall
The position of the tube tip
cards.explain: The sensor senses tip position, not pressure directly.

cards.question: Which effect do suitable bearings, clean construction of all moving parts and, in the altimeter, support with vibration guard against
options: hysteresis
backlash
friction
cards.explain: Those three measures are the ones named for keeping friction to a minimum.

cards.question: Of the two capsule error influences, which one depends on whether the pressure was rising or falling
options: the elastic aftereffect
the hysteresis
the effect of temperature
cards.explain: Hysteresis is the difference between the rising and the falling pressure curve, while the elastic aftereffect comes from pressure held constant over a long time.

cards.question: A diaphragm capsule delivers only a stroke of 4 to 5 mm with a small force. What must the transfer mechanism do with it?
options: Convert it into a damped rotation of the needle
Convert it into an amplified stroke of the capsule
Convert it into an amplified rotation of the needle
cards.explain: The mechanism amplifies the tiny stroke into needle rotation.

cards.question: Which effect does friction have in the transfer mechanism of an aneroid instrument
options: It falsifies the measured result
It damps the capsule stroke
It raises the capsule hysteresis
cards.explain: Friction in the mechanism corrupts the reading.

cards.question: How is friction in the indicator mechanism kept to a minimum
options: With suitable bearings and clean construction of all moving parts
With sealed bearings and grease filling of all moving parts
With heavier levers and increased spring tension on all moving parts
cards.explain: Good bearings and clean mechanical construction minimise friction.

cards.question: In the altimeter one further measure helps to reduce the effect of friction. Which measure is this?
options: Vibration of the instrument
Balancing of the needle
Damping of the capsule
cards.explain: Vibration keeps the altimeter mechanism from sticking, helping against friction.

cards.question: Play in the gearing between the pinion and the tooth segment would falsify the indication. How is this play taken out?
options: By increased bearing clearance
By spring tension on both sides
By spring tension on one side
cards.explain: A one-sided spring tension takes up the gear backlash.

cards.question: What is meant by the hysteresis of a membrane capsule
options: The stroke lags behind the pressure when a constant pressure acts for a long time
The curve with increasing pressure differs from the curve with decreasing pressure
The curve with increasing pressure differs from the curve with increasing temperature
cards.explain: Hysteresis is the difference between the rising and falling pressure characteristics.

cards.question: What causes the elastic aftereffect of a capsule
options: A rapidly changing pressure acting on the capsule during a climb
A temperature change acting on the capsule mounting
A constant pressure acting on the capsule over a longer period of time
cards.explain: Long-held constant pressure makes the capsule yield slowly.

cards.question: What is the result of the slow yielding of a capsule under constant pressure
options: A time lag in the stroke
A permanent offset of the needle
A change of the residual pressure
cards.explain: The stroke lags in time, which is the elastic aftereffect.

cards.question: Friction in the transfer mechanism, hysteresis, elastic aftereffect and temperature all work against precise operation. Which instruments do these error influences affect?
options: All aneroid type instruments
Only metric scale altimeters
Only digital air data computers
cards.explain: The manual states these errors act on all aneroid instruments.

cards.question: Static pressure acting on the capsule of an aneroid altimeter produces a stroke of only a few millimetres with a small force. Which part makes this usable for the indication
options: the pressure scale, which sets the reference level
the position sensor, which converts it into an electrical signal
the transfer mechanism, which amplifies it into rotation of the needle
cards.explain: Static pressure moves the capsule only a few millimetres, so the transfer mechanism has to turn that small stroke into an amplified needle rotation.

cards.question: The synchro transmitter of a Bourdon tube transducer is found unserviceable while the tube itself is sound. Which part of the conversion is lost?
options: The supply of static pressure to the curved tube
The deformation of the curved tube by the applied pressure
The conversion of the tube tip position into an electrical signal
cards.explain: The synchro transmitter is the position sensor, so with it unserviceable the tube tip still moves but its position is no longer turned into an electrical signal.

cards.question: An altimeter needle must turn 51 times over its full range. Which demand does this place on the instrument?
options: The highest demands on case sealing and static line length
The highest demands on material and fine mechanical precision
The highest demands on electrical power and signal bandwidth
cards.explain: Such fine resolution needs the best material and fine mechanics.

cards.question: The spring that holds one side of the gearing under tension is found broken in an aneroid instrument. Which error influence is no longer compensated?
options: Hysteresis of the membrane capsule
Backlash between the pinions and the tooth segments
Friction in the bearings of the moving parts
cards.explain: The one-sided spring tension is what takes out the backlash in the gearing, so a broken spring leaves that backlash uncompensated.

cards.question: Which measures are used to characterize the properties of a capsule for its intended use
options: Special coatings, artificial ageing and particular bearing materials
Special alloys, natural ageing and particular residual pressures
Special alloys, artificial ageing and particular waveforms
cards.explain: The three listed measures are special alloys, artificial ageing and particular waveforms.

cards.question: Which parts make temperature compensation demanding over the range -70 to +50 degrees C
options: The capsule mounting and the flexible tubes in the static system
The capsule mounting and the variable steering levers in the indicator mechanism
The pinion bearings and the quick release connectors of the instrument
cards.explain: Compensation is hard because of the capsule mounting and the variable steering levers.

cards.question: An altimeter is held at one steady pressure on the test bench for a long time and the indication slowly drifts. Which error influence explains this?
options: The backlash of the pinion gearing
The elastic aftereffect of the capsule
The hysteresis of the capsule
cards.explain: Slow drift under a constant held pressure is the elastic aftereffect, not hysteresis.

cards.question: An altimeter reads slightly differently at the same test pressure depending on whether the pressure was raised or lowered to reach it. Which error influence is shown?
options: Friction in the transfer mechanism
Elastic aftereffect of the diaphragm capsule
Hysteresis of the diaphragm capsule
cards.explain: A difference between the rising and falling approach to the same pressure is hysteresis.

cards.question: Through which parts must the smallest pressure change act to deflect the needle exactly
options: From the capsule via bellows, resonator and coil
From the capsule via levers, shaft and cogwheel
From the diaphragm via strain gauges, bridge and amplifier
cards.explain: The mechanical chain runs capsule, levers, shaft, cogwheel, needle.

cards.question: What is the function of a pressure transducer
options: To convert electrical signals into measured pressures
To convert measured pressures into mechanical needle movement
To convert measured pressures into electrical signals
cards.explain: Transducers turn pressure into electrical signals.

cards.question: In which equipment are pressure transducers used
options: In air data computers
In flight control computers
In inertial reference units
cards.explain: The manual names air data computers as an application.

cards.question: Several electronic pressure sensor principles exist. Which one is described as the most commonly used?
options: The vibrating transducer
The force compensated cell
The piezoresistive transducer
cards.explain: The manual calls the vibrating transducer the most commonly used type.

cards.question: From which material is the micromechanical pressure transducer chamber made
options: Silicon material
Metal material
Pyrex material
cards.explain: The chamber is made of silicon.

cards.question: What is the size of the micromechanical pressure transducer structure
options: Only a few micrometres
Only a few centimetres
Only a few millimetres
cards.explain: The structure measures only a few millimetres.

cards.question: How many strain gauges are normally fitted on the diaphragm of a piezoresistive transducer
options: Two resistors
Eight resistors
Four resistors
cards.explain: Normally four strain gauges are used.

cards.question: Pressure transducers are fitted in air data computers because the computer needs the measured pressures in which form
options: as electrical signals
as an output frequency of the indicator
as amplified needle rotations
cards.explain: A transducer turns the measured pressures into electrical signals, which is the form the air data computer works with.

cards.question: Pressure transducers have converted the measured pressures into electrical signals. What happens with these signals next?
options: They are sent to the computer and transformed into the required output signals
They are sent to the probe heater and transformed into the required current
They are sent to the indicator and transformed into the required needle deflection
cards.explain: The signals go to the computer, which makes the required outputs.

cards.question: What does the output frequency generated by a vibrating transducer depend on
options: the supply voltage
the input pressure
the reference chamber vacuum
cards.explain: The frequency the vibrating transducer puts out is set by the pressure fed into it.

cards.question: Which output does a vibrating transducer generate
options: An output frequency which depends on the input pressure
An output voltage which depends on the input pressure
An output frequency which depends on the reference pressure
cards.explain: Its output is a frequency that varies with the measured pressure.

cards.question: Which function does the outer case of a vibrating transducer have
options: It forms the outer wall of the measured pressure chamber
It forms the inner wall of the reference pressure chamber
It forms the outer wall of the reference pressure chamber
cards.explain: The outer case is the outer wall of the reference chamber.

cards.question: Which type of barometer chamber is the micromechanical pressure transducer built like
options: the liquid-based type
the mercury type
the aneroid type
cards.explain: Although it is made of silicon, the micromechanical transducer is described as an aneroid-type chamber.

cards.question: What happens when pressure acts on the silicon lid of a piezoresistive transducer
options: The lid is dented and the resistance in its surface changes
The lid vibrates and the frequency of its surface changes
The lid is dented and the capacitance in its surface changes
cards.explain: Denting the lid deforms the surface resistors and changes their resistance.

cards.question: What is the output voltage of a piezoresistive transducer proportional to
options: The reference pressure
The supply frequency
The input pressure
cards.explain: The output voltage rises in proportion to the applied pressure.

cards.question: The four strain gages on the diaphragm have to produce one measuring voltage. In which configuration are they connected?
options: A wheatstone bridge
A follow-up linkage
A synchro transmitter
cards.explain: The normally four strain gages of the diaphragm are connected in a wheatstone bridge configuration.

cards.question: How are the four strain gauges distributed on the base plate
options: All four on the front side of the plate
Three on the front side and one on the back side
Two on the front side and two on the back side
cards.explain: Two gauges sit on the front and two on the back.

cards.question: A force compensated pressure cell is fitted instead of a plain pressure cell. Which two advantages are gained?
options: It is sensitive to pressure changes and has small instrument errors
It is insensitive to pressure changes and has small instrument errors
It is insensitive to pressure changes and needs no separate pressure cells
cards.explain: The force compensated cell is insensitive to pressure changes and keeps instrument errors small.

cards.question: Which pressure sensing type is listed as needing no different pressure cells for static and pitot?
options: The force compensated pressure cell
The vibration pressure transducer
The plain pressure cell type
cards.explain: The table gives 'no different pressure cells for static and pitot' for the vibration type; both pressure cell types are listed as needing different cells for static and pitot.

cards.question: An electronic pressure sensor delivers an output frequency that depends on the input pressure. Which sensor is this
options: the piezoresistive transducer, the most commonly used type
the vibrating transducer, the most commonly used type
the pressure cell transducer, the most commonly used type
cards.explain: The vibrating transducer is named as the most commonly used type and it is the one whose output frequency depends on the input pressure.

cards.question: One transducer gives an output frequency depending on the input pressure, another an output voltage in proportion to the input pressure. Which two transducers are these
options: the vibrating transducer and the micromechanical transducer respectively
the micromechanical transducer and the vibrating transducer respectively
the vibrating transducer and the Bourdon tube transducer respectively
cards.explain: The vibrating transducer produces a frequency; the micromechanical transducer produces a voltage in proportion to the pressure.

cards.question: A vibrating transducer is cut open. Where is the pressure that is being measured found?
options: In the reference chamber outside the vibrating cylinder
In the pressure chamber inside the center body
In the pressure chamber inside the vibrating cylinder
cards.explain: The measured pressure sits in the chamber inside the cylinder.

cards.question: What is done with the signal from the pickup coil
options: It is amplified and used as output, and fed back to the reference chamber
It is digitized and used as reference, and fed back to the drive coil
It is amplified and used as output, and fed back to the drive coil
cards.explain: The pickup signal serves both as the amplified output and as the feedback to the drive coil.

cards.question: Why is the pickup coil signal fed back to the drive coil of a vibrating transducer?
options: To keep the reference chamber at a constant vacuum
To keep the output frequency at a constant value
To keep the cylinder vibrating with its natural frequency
cards.explain: The feedback loop sustains vibration at the natural frequency.

cards.question: A pressure sensor consists of a chamber made of silicon, only a few millimetres in size. Which sensor is this, and how is its chamber built
options: the micromechanical transducer, built as a liquid-based chamber
the vibrating transducer, built as an aneroid-type chamber
the micromechanical transducer, built as an aneroid-type chamber
cards.explain: The micromechanical transducer is the aneroid-type chamber made of silicon whose structure is only a few millimetres in size.

cards.question: Pressure bends the diaphragm of a piezoresistive transducer and the resistance of the strain gages changes. What does the bridge then deliver, and what is it proportional to?
options: An output frequency, in proportion to the input pressure
An output voltage, in proportion to the input pressure
An output voltage, in proportion to the supply voltage
cards.explain: The four strain gages sit in a wheatstone bridge, and the change in their resistance gives an output voltage in proportion to the input pressure.

cards.question: Pressure is applied to a piezoresistive transducer. How do the two bridge voltages behave?
options: U1 decreases while U2 increases
U1 increases while U2 decreases
U1 and U2 both increase
cards.explain: The two halves of the bridge move in opposite directions when the plate bends.

cards.question: A strain gauge wire is made thicker while its length stays the same. How does its resistance change?
options: It is independent of the area
It increases with increasing area
It decreases with increasing area
cards.explain: A larger cross section lowers the resistance.

cards.question: A strain gauge on the bent side of the diaphragm is stretched. Why does its resistance rise?
options: Because the material constant of the wire rises with the strain
Because the wire becomes shorter and its cross section larger
Because the wire becomes longer and its cross section smaller
cards.explain: Figure 35 shows the stretched side getting longer and thinner, and R = rho x l / A, so both changes raise the resistance.

cards.question: Which pressure is used by an altimeter
options: Static pressure only
Pitot and static pressure
Pitot pressure only
cards.explain: The manual states the altimeter works on static pressure alone.

cards.question: An airspeed indicator in a simple system is connected to two pressure lines. Which pressures does it use?
options: Static pressure and differential pressure
Pitot pressure and total pressure
Pitot pressure and static pressure
cards.explain: The airspeed indicator is the only one of the three that needs both pitot and static pressure.

cards.question: How many separate pitot-static pressure systems are installed on modern commercial aircraft
options: Three or four separate systems
One or two separate systems
Two or three separate systems
cards.explain: The manual gives two or three separate systems.

cards.question: What is static pressure
options: The actual atmospheric pressure surrounding the aircraft
The build-up of air pressure in a tube facing the airstream
The difference between total pressure and ram pressure
cards.explain: Static pressure is simply the ambient atmospheric pressure around the aircraft.

cards.question: A pneumatic device is calibrated to the international standard atmosphere. Which value of air density at mean sea level applies?
cards.explain: The ISA sea level density given in the manual is 1,225 kg/m3.

cards.question: What does the abbreviation SSE stand for
options: Static source error
Standard source error
Static system error
cards.explain: SSE is the static source error.

cards.question: What is pitot pressure
options: The build-up of air pressure in a tube with its opening facing the airstream
The build-up of air pressure in a tube with its opening across the airstream
The actual atmospheric pressure in the air surrounding the aircraft
cards.explain: Pitot pressure builds up in a tube whose opening points into the airstream.

cards.question: Which two pressures make up the total pressure Ptot
options: Ram pressure and differential pressure
Static pressure and differential pressure
Ram pressure and static pressure
cards.explain: The manual gives total pressure as ram pressure plus static pressure.

cards.question: Where is the pitot tube usually located on the aircraft
options: Near the nose, on the nose itself or below the cockpit
Near the tail, on the fin itself or below the rudder
Near the nose, on the wing leading edge or below the flaps
cards.explain: These are the three locations the manual names.

cards.question: What does the pitot tube consist of and which pressure is present in it during the entire flight
options: A flapper plate chamber in which total pressure Ptot is present
A cylindrical pipe in which total pressure Ptot is present
A cylindrical pipe in which static pressure Ps is present
cards.explain: It is a cylindrical pipe carrying total pressure throughout the flight.

cards.question: Why is the Prandtl tube electrically heated
options: To prevent condensation
To prevent deformation
To prevent icing
cards.explain: Electrical heating keeps the probe free of ice.

cards.question: A Prandtl tube supplies both pressures from one probe. Where is it located on the aircraft?
options: Under the wing of the aircraft
At the rear of the aircraft
At the front of the aircraft
cards.explain: It sits at the front, like the pitot tube.

cards.question: An air data system receives three parameters from one single multi function probe. Which parameters are they?
options: Angle of sideslip, total air temperature and total pressure
Angle of attack, total air temperature and total pressure
Angle of attack, static air temperature and static pressure
cards.explain: AOA, TAT and total pressure are the three outputs of the probe.

cards.question: Which part of the multi function probe measures the angle of attack
options: A wind vane
A TAT tube
A pitot probe
cards.explain: The wind vane is the AOA sensing element.

cards.question: What do the altimeter and the vertical speed indicator have in common
options: Both use pitot pressure
Both use pitot pressure and static pressure
Both use static pressure
cards.explain: Static pressure is named as the pressure used by each of these two instruments.

cards.question: Why are the left and right hand static pressure measuring locations of one static system connected to each other
options: To increase the pressure delivered to the connected instruments
To drain any water collected inside the static pressure lines
To compensate for any unbalance in pressure measurement
cards.explain: Cross-connecting the two sides evens out an unbalanced pressure reading between them.

cards.question: Compared with the simple system of a small aircraft, what does a modern commercial aircraft have
options: One pitot system feeding two static systems
One pitot system and one static system as well
Two or three separate pitot-static pressure systems
cards.explain: The simple system has one of each, whereas the modern commercial aircraft has two or three separate systems.

cards.question: Why are modern commercial aircraft fitted with separate pitot-static pressure systems
options: For weight reasons
For calibration reasons
For safety reasons
cards.explain: Redundant systems are installed for safety.

cards.question: What does the alternate static source selector valve allow the Captain to do
options: Use the copilot's static pressure system
Use the copilot's pitot pressure system
Isolate the copilot's static pressure system
cards.explain: The valve switches the Captain over to the copilot's static source.

cards.question: The Captain's static system becomes faulty in flight. Which statement about switching over to the auxiliary system by means of the static air source selector valve is correct?
options: Only on a few aircraft types can the indicators be switched to the pitot system
Only on a few aircraft types can the indicators be switched to the auxiliary system
On every aircraft type the indicators can be switched to the auxiliary system
cards.explain: The manual restricts this switching possibility to a few aircraft types only.

cards.question: Between what does the handle of the static source selector valve choose for the instruments
options: Normal static pressure and alternate static pressure
Normal static pressure and pitot pressure
Alternate static pressure and pitot pressure
cards.explain: The valve is connected to a normal and an alternate static pressure supply and passes one of them to the instruments.

cards.question: Why are static ports made flush with the skin of the aircraft
options: The surface stays smooth and no pressure distorting turbulences occur
Water entering the ports is drained away again
The ports can be heated electrically from inside the skin
cards.explain: A flush port keeps the zone smooth, which is what the warning requires so that no pressure distorting turbulences arise.

cards.question: On which two quantities does air pressure p depend
options: Air density and mach number
Air density and temperature
Temperature and angle of attack
cards.explain: The manual lists air density and temperature as the two quantities.

cards.question: What is done with the ISA values defined at mean sea level
options: All pneumatic devices are corrected according to the flap position
All pneumatic devices are calibrated according to these values
All pneumatic devices are heated according to these values
cards.explain: The ISA values are the calibration reference for pneumatic devices.

cards.question: What do aircraft manufacturers ensure when they choose the position of the static ports
options: That they lie in areas with high turbulence and ram air distortion
That they lie in areas with low turbulence and ram air distortion
That they lie in areas with low temperature and air density variation
cards.explain: Low turbulence and low ram air distortion keep the static reading true.

cards.question: A technician is told that the static port zones must be absolutely clean and have a smooth surface. Which reason does the warning give?
options: So that no pressure distorting turbulences can occur
So that no electrical heating current can be lost
So that no water can enter the connected pressure lines
cards.explain: Dirt or roughness creates turbulence that distorts the sensed pressure.

cards.question: Why do most helicopters have special cover plates at the static ports
options: To compensate the effects caused by the strong vibration of the rotor
To compensate the effects caused by the high angle of attack of the rotor
To compensate the effects caused by the strong downwash of the rotor
cards.explain: The cover plates offset the pressure effects of the rotor downwash.

cards.question: Among the factors the static source error depends on, which one is qualified as applying only where relevant
options: The angle of attack
The position of the flaps
The mach number
cards.explain: The angle of attack is the item carrying the qualification if applicable.

cards.question: Why can a static source error arise on an aircraft
options: It is not always possible to calibrate the pneumatic devices to the ISA values
It is not always possible to find turbulence and ram air free zones on the aircraft
It is not always possible to keep the static ports electrically heated in flight
cards.explain: Where no turbulence free and ram air free zone exists, the sensed static pressure is falsified.

cards.question: An engineer is told that the static source error of a jet aeroplane is not a constant value. On which factors does it depend?
options: The mach number, the angle of attack, the rudder position and the nose gear position
The mach number, the angle of attack, the flap position and the nose gear position
The mach number, the air density, the flap position and the outside air temperature
cards.explain: These four items are the dependencies the manual lists for the SSE.

cards.question: How large is the static source error on slow-flying propeller planes
options: So large that it must be corrected
So small that it must be measured
So small that it is negligible
cards.explain: At low speed the error is negligible.

cards.question: The crew has to obtain the correct value from the distorted values being displayed. Where are the correction tables found?
options: In the Operating Manual or in the flight regulations
In the Operating Manual or in the weight and balance data
In the Aircraft Maintenance Manual or in the flight log
cards.explain: The manual names the Operating Manual and the flight regulations as the sources of the correction tables.

cards.question: Which pressure reading is affected by a static source error
options: The total pressure reading
The ram pressure reading
The static pressure reading
cards.explain: The SSE falsifies the static pressure reading.

cards.question: The static source error is listed with several dependencies. Which of them is marked as unusual?
options: The angle of attack
The position of the nose gear
The position of the flaps
cards.explain: Only the nose gear position carries the remark unusual.

cards.question: Why does the static pressure have to be known before the ram pressure can be obtained
options: Static pressure and ram pressure are measured by the same probe
Total pressure is made up of ram pressure plus static pressure
Ram pressure is the atmospheric pressure surrounding the aircraft
cards.explain: Since total pressure is the sum of ram and static pressure, the static part must be known so that it can be taken out.

cards.question: What is the difference between total pressure and ram pressure
options: Total pressure also contains the static pressure
Total pressure is measured at the static ports
Total pressure also contains the dynamic pressure
cards.explain: Total pressure is ram pressure together with static pressure, so the static part is what it holds in addition.

cards.question: Which pressure alone is required to measure the speed of the aircraft in relation to the ambient air
options: The static pressure ps
The ram pressure q
The total pressure Ptot
cards.explain: Only the dynamic or ram pressure q is needed for speed measurement.

cards.question: How is ram pressure q obtained in the instrument
options: By measuring the sum of the total pressure and the static pressure
By measuring the differential pressure between total and static pressure
By measuring the static pressure at two separate static ports
cards.explain: Ram pressure is the difference between total and static pressure.

cards.question: Ram pressure cannot be sensed on its own. Which pressure is already known from the static ports and is used to obtain it?
options: The static pressure ps
The total pressure Ptot
The dynamic pressure q
cards.explain: The static ports supply ps, which is subtracted from Ptot to leave q.

cards.question: How does the electrical heating of the pitot tube compare with that of the static ports
options: The pitot tube is heated, while only some aircraft types have heated static ports
Only the static ports are heated, the pitot tube being self draining
Both are heated on every aircraft type
cards.explain: Heating is stated plainly for the pitot tube, whereas heated static ports are stated only for some aircraft types.

cards.question: Why is a pitot tube aligned towards the predetermined airstream
options: The airstream keeps the drain hole clear of water
The airstream stops the tube from freezing up
Pitot pressure builds up in a tube whose opening faces the airstream
cards.explain: Pitot pressure only builds up when the opening of the tube faces the airstream, so the alignment is what produces the pressure.

cards.question: A pitot tube is being refitted to an aeroplane after removal. How must it be aligned?
options: So that it faces the predetermined rotor downwash
So that it lies across the predetermined airstream
So that it faces the predetermined airstream
cards.explain: The tube must point into the airstream to build up total pressure.

cards.question: What do the small drain hole and the baffle of a pitot tube ensure
options: That ram air entering the tube is slowed down
That water entering the tube is drained away
That the tube inlet is kept free of any deformation
cards.explain: Their job is to get rid of water that has entered the tube.

cards.question: A student is worried that the drain hole in a pitot tube lets pressure escape. Which statement from the manual answers this?
options: The drain hole and the baffle slightly reduce the total pressure
The drain hole and the baffle do not affect the total pressure
The drain hole and the baffle slightly reduce the static pressure
cards.explain: The manual states in brackets that they do not affect the total pressure.

cards.question: During a walk-around a technician finds a small dent at the inlet of a pitot tube. Which instruction from the manual applies?
options: The tube inlet must not display any signs of deformation whatsoever
The tube inlet may display slight deformation if the drain hole is clear
The tube inlet may display slight deformation if the heating is serviceable
cards.explain: The manual allows no deformation of the inlet at all.

cards.question: Why is the Prandtl tube called a pitot-static-tube
options: It is fitted at the front of the aircraft like a pitot tube
It combines a pitot tube with a sensor to measure static pressure
It is heated electrically like the static ports
cards.explain: The name follows from the tube holding both a pitot tube and a static pressure sensor in one unit.

cards.question: How does the fitting position of the Prandtl tube compare with that of the pitot tube
options: The Prandtl tube is located in the same way as the pitot tube at the front of the aircraft
The Prandtl tube is located on the sides of the fuselage and the pitot tube at the front
The Prandtl tube is located below the rotor and the pitot tube at the front
cards.explain: The two probes are fitted the same way, at the front of the aircraft.

cards.question: On a Prandtl tube, what do the cylindrical inlet and the holes drilled in the sides supply, in that order
options: The total pressure and the connected static lines
The total pressure and the drain line
The connected static lines and the total pressure
cards.explain: Total pressure enters at the cylindrical inlet while the side holes feed the static lines.

cards.question: What does the Prandtl tube combine in one unit
options: A pitot tube with a sensor to measure static pressure
A pitot tube with a sensor to measure total air temperature
A static port with a sensor to measure the angle of attack
cards.explain: It puts the pitot function and a static pressure sensor into one probe.

cards.question: A Prandtl tube has a cylindrical inlet at the front and a row of holes drilled in its sides. What do these side holes supply?
options: Drainage for one or two connected water traps
Information for one or two connected static lines
Information for one or two connected pitot lines
cards.explain: The side holes feed the static lines, while the front inlet feeds total pressure.

cards.question: What do the flapper plate and drain hole of a Prandtl tube prevent
options: Water from entering the pitot line
Icing from forming at the tube inlet
Roughness from forming on the tube surface
cards.explain: They keep water out of the pitot line.

cards.question: A Prandtl tube is found with a rough surface after a repair. Which consequence does the manual warn about?
options: It will lead to total pressure errors
It will lead to static pressure errors
It will lead to heating element failures
cards.explain: Roughness disturbs the flow over the side holes and falsifies static pressure.

cards.question: How does a Prandtl tube obtain the ram pressure and static pressure needed for speed indication
options: From one single ram air tube
From two connected static ports
From two separate measuring points
cards.explain: The Prandtl tube takes both pressures at one single tube.

cards.question: Which two separate measuring points does the Prandtl tube replace
options: The pitot tube and the air data computer
The pitot tube and the static port
The static port and the difference bellows
cards.explain: The manual names the pitot tube and the static port as the two points it replaces.

cards.question: A Prandtl tube delivers total pressure and static pressure. Where is the required differential pressure obtained?
options: In the static port or in the drain hole
In the tube itself or in the piping
In the instrument or in a computer
cards.explain: The subtraction is done in the instrument or in a computer, not in the probe.

cards.question: A multi function probe must deliver the total pressure to the air data system. Which of its parts provides this parameter?
options: The temperature tube
The pitot probe
The wind vane
cards.explain: The built-in pitot probe supplies the total pressure.

cards.question: Each multi function probe has to pass its measured data to the related computer. Through which item does it do so?
options: Through the digital converter
Through the air data computer
Through the difference bellows
cards.explain: The digital converter is the link between the probe and the related computer.

cards.question: How are the two pneumatic back up instruments arranged in some aircraft types
options: Both functions are integrated in one instrument
Only the altitude function is retained
Both functions are shared between three instruments
cards.explain: The two standby functions can be brought together in a single instrument on some types.

cards.question: The pitot probe of a simple system becomes completely blocked while the static system stays clear. Which of the three supplied instruments is affected?
options: The altimeter
The vertical speed indicator
The airspeed indicator
cards.explain: Of the three instruments only the airspeed indicator uses pitot pressure, so only it depends on the pitot probe.

cards.question: Which instrument of the simple system needs a pressure connection in addition to the static system
options: The vertical speed indicator
The altimeter
The airspeed indicator
cards.explain: The altimeter and vertical speed indicator use static pressure only, while the airspeed indicator also needs pitot pressure.

cards.question: During a repair the connection between the left and right hand measuring locations of one static pressure system is left open. What is lost by this?
options: The supply of pitot pressure to the instruments
The compensation for any unbalance in pressure measurement
The heating of the static measuring locations
cards.explain: The two locations are joined only to compensate unbalance in pressure measurement, so breaking the joint removes that compensation.

cards.question: A technician traces one static pressure system of a small aeroplane and finds a measuring location on the left and on the right hand side of the fuselage. Which statement describes this arrangement correctly?
options: Each location belongs to a separate static system and they stay isolated
Both locations belong to the same static system and are connected together
Both locations belong to the same pitot system and are connected together
cards.explain: One static system uses both side locations and they are joined to each other.

cards.question: The Captain moves the handle of the alternate static source selector valve to its other position. Which static pressure then reaches his instruments?
options: The copilot's static pressure system
His own static pressure system
The pitot pressure of his own system
cards.explain: The valve exists so that the Captain can take his static pressure from the copilot's system instead of his own.

cards.question: An aeroplane has a fault in one pilot's static system and is not one of the few types that can be switched to the auxiliary system. Which possibility remains?
options: Use of the other pilot's static system via the selector valve
Use of the pitot system via the selector valve
Use of the auxiliary system via the selector valve
cards.explain: Switching to the auxiliary system is limited to a few types, so the cross-over to the other pilot's static system is what remains.

cards.question: A helicopter cannot keep its static ports in air that is free of rotor downwash. Which fitting deals with this?
options: Special cover plates at the static ports
A drain hole at each static port
Electrically heated static ports
cards.explain: The cover plates are fitted for exactly this purpose, to compensate the effects of the strong rotor downwash at the ports.

cards.question: After a skin repair the zone around a static port is left with a rough surface. What must be expected at that port?
options: A blockage of the pressure pipe
A loss of the port heating
