Pressure distorting turbulences
cards.explain: The zone is required to be smooth precisely so that no pressure distorting turbulences occur, so a rough surface allows them.

cards.question: Why are static ports placed in areas with low turbulence and ram air distortion
options: Because turbulence and ram air distortion overheat the static port zones
Because turbulence and ram air distortion falsify the static pressure reading
Because turbulence and ram air distortion block the static pressure hoses
cards.explain: Where such zones cannot be found the static pressure reading is affected, so a quiet zone keeps the reading true.

cards.question: An aeroplane extends its flaps on the approach. Which reading can change as a result of this alone?
options: The static pressure reading
The total air temperature reading
The angle of attack reading
cards.explain: The static source error depends on the position of the flaps, and it is the static pressure reading that this error affects.

cards.question: Of the factors the static source error depends on, which two change with the configuration of the aircraft
options: The mach number and the position of the flaps
The position of the flaps and the position of the nose gear
The mach number and the angle of attack
cards.explain: Flaps and nose gear are the two listed items that are set by the aircraft configuration, the other two being flight condition values.

cards.question: An aeroplane changes its angle of attack in cruise with everything else unchanged. Which measurement may be affected by this?
options: The total pressure measurement
The pitot pressure measurement
The static pressure measurement
cards.explain: The angle of attack is one of the factors the static source error depends on, and that error affects the static pressure reading.

cards.question: A slow-flying propeller plane and a jet aeroplane near the speed of sound differ in one of the listed static source error factors above all. Which factor is that?
options: The position of the flaps
The position of the nose gear
The mach number
cards.explain: The two cases are set apart by how near the speed of sound they fly, which is the mach number among the listed factors.

cards.question: A jet aeroplane flies near to the speed of sound and its static source error exceeds the tolerances required by law. Which correction becomes necessary?
options: A correction using an alternate static source valve
A correction using an air data computer
A correction using a differential pressure bellows
cards.explain: The manual calls for an air data computer correction in this case.

cards.question: A static source error falsifies the static pressure supplied to a simple pitot-static system. Which instruments are affected?
options: All three instruments of the simple system
Only the vertical speed indicator of the system
Only the airspeed indicator of the system
cards.explain: All three instruments of the simple system are supplied with static pressure, so all three are affected.

cards.question: A slow-flying propeller aeroplane and a jet aeroplane near the speed of sound both have a static source error. Which comparison is correct?
options: Negligible on the jet aeroplane and possibly beyond the legal tolerance on the propeller plane
Beyond the legal tolerance on both aeroplanes and corrected by the air data computer
Negligible on the propeller aeroplane and possibly beyond the legal tolerance on the jet
cards.explain: The manual calls the error negligible at low speed and possibly beyond the legal tolerance near the speed of sound.

cards.question: In the relation Ptot = q + ps, where is the quantity ps delivered to the instrument from
options: The static ports
The pitot probe
The drain hole of the pitot tube
cards.explain: The static pressure ps used in the relation is the pressure measured at the static ports.

cards.question: Why is an airspeed indicator fed from the pitot probe as well as the static system
options: The static pressure alone gives the speed in the surrounding air
The pitot probe cannot deliver a pressure without a static reference
The ram pressure it needs is the total pressure less the static pressure
cards.explain: Speed needs the ram pressure, and the ram pressure is obtained by subtracting the static pressure from the total pressure delivered by the pitot probe.

cards.question: A pitot tube delivers the pressure present in its cylindrical pipe throughout the flight. What must be supplied in addition before a speed can be obtained?
options: The total air temperature from a temperature probe
The static pressure from the static ports
A second total pressure from another pitot tube
cards.explain: The pitot tube gives total pressure only, and the static pressure from the static ports has to be subtracted from it to get the ram pressure.

cards.question: An aircraft type is to take both the ram pressure and the static pressure needed for speed indication from one single ram air tube. Which probe is used?
options: A multi function probe
A pitot tube
A Prandtl tube
cards.explain: The Prandtl tube is the single ram air tube that supplies both of these pressures.

cards.question: Which feature does a Prandtl tube carry that a plain pitot tube does not
options: Holes drilled in the sides supplying connected static lines
A cylindrical inlet for the total pressure
Electrical heating of the tube
cards.explain: Both probes have a cylindrical pipe and electrical heating, but the side holes feeding static lines belong to the Prandtl tube.

cards.question: Both a pitot tube and a Prandtl tube keep water out of the pitot line. Which item does this in the Prandtl tube together with the drain hole?
options: A flapper plate
A cover plate
A baffle
cards.explain: The Prandtl tube works with a flapper plate and a drain hole, the baffle being the item named for the pitot tube.

cards.question: On an aircraft type fitted with a Prandtl tube, where does the static pressure needed for speed indication come from
options: The same single ram air tube that supplies the ram pressure
The cylindrical inlet at the front of the tube
A pair of static ports on the sides of the fuselage
cards.explain: On these types the two pressures come from the one Prandtl tube instead of separate pitot tube and static port.

cards.question: A Prandtl tube delivers total pressure and static pressure to a computer. Which quantity does the computer obtain from them, and what is it needed for?
options: The ram pressure, needed for the speed indication
The static source error, needed for the altitude indication
The total air temperature, needed for the speed indication
cards.explain: The differential of the two delivered pressures is the ram pressure q, which is what the speed indication requires.

cards.question: An air data system is to receive the angle of attack from the same probe that gives it the total pressure. Which probe meets this?
options: A Prandtl tube
A multi function probe
A pitot tube
cards.explain: Only the multi function probe is stated to give angle of attack as well as total pressure.

cards.question: A multi function probe delivers the total pressure to the air data system. Which quantity is still required for a speed indication
options: The static pressure
The angle of attack
The total air temperature
cards.explain: The ram pressure needed for speed is the total pressure less the static pressure, and the probe supplies only the total pressure of the two.

cards.question: An aircraft with a modern EFIS carries two pneumatic back up instruments. Which of them has to be connected to the pitot system?
options: The standby altimeter
Both of them equally
The standby airspeed indicator
cards.explain: An airspeed indicator uses pitot pressure as well as static pressure, while an altimeter uses static pressure only.

cards.question: With what must the standby altimeter fitted as a back up in an EFIS aircraft be supplied
options: Pitot pressure only
Pitot pressure and static pressure
Static pressure only
cards.explain: It is a pneumatic altimeter, and an altimeter works on static pressure alone.

cards.question: Which colour is used to designate pitot system connections
options: Yellow
Red
Blue
cards.explain: Pitot connections carry the red designation; yellow belongs to the static side.

cards.question: Two lines are parted at a quick-disconnect during maintenance. What happens at the coupling?
options: It vents the line to ambient air
It seals itself
It stays open until a cap is fitted
cards.explain: A self-sealing coupling closes the line itself the moment it is parted.

cards.question: A technician must check the mouth of a static port against its limits. Where are these limits normally found?
options: In ATA chapter 21
In ATA chapter 31
In ATA chapter 34
cards.explain: The manual points to ATA chapter 34 for the static port mouth limits.

cards.question: A technician must assess damage to the skin next to a static port. Which equipment is used?
options: A scale and a feeler-gage
A straight edge and a torque wrench
A scale and a depth micrometer
cards.explain: The manual names the scale and the feeler-gage as the assessment tools.

cards.question: Which system controls the cabin rate
options: The anti-ice system
The pitot static system
The airconditioning system
cards.explain: The manual names the airconditioning system as the controller of cabin rate.

cards.question: Which instrument is affected by a leakage in the pitot system
options: The vertical speed indicator only
The airspeed indicator only
The altimeter only
cards.explain: Only the airspeed indicator is fed from the pitot system.

cards.question: What do the altimeter and the vertical speed indicator indicate during a climb with a blocked static system
options: The altimeter increases and the vertical speed indication stays at zero
The altimeter holds the same altitude and the vertical speed indication stays at zero
The altimeter holds the same altitude and the vertical speed indication rises
cards.explain: With static pressure trapped, neither instrument can register the climb.

cards.question: What does the vertical speed indicator indicate during a descent with a blocked static system
options: A steady rate of descent
A zero rate
A steady rate of climb
cards.explain: The trapped static pressure never changes, so the VSI sees no rate at all.

cards.question: What does a completely blocked pitot tube mean
options: The inlet and the drain hole are blocked
The inlet is blocked and the drain hole is open
The drain hole is blocked and the inlet is open
cards.explain: Complete blockage covers both the inlet and the drain hole.

cards.question: A pitot tube is completely blocked by ice. Which instruments are not affected?
options: The airspeed indicator and the vertical speed indicator
The altimeter and the airspeed indicator
The altimeter and the vertical speed indicator
cards.explain: Those two run on static pressure, which the pitot blockage does not touch.

cards.question: The pitot inlet is blocked by ice but the water drain hole is still open. What does the airspeed indication do?
options: It increases into the overspeed region
It decreases to zero
It stays unchanged at the last value
cards.explain: With pitot pressure equal to static pressure the airspeed indicator reads zero.

cards.question: The indications fluctuate during a check of the pitot static system. What does this show?
options: The presence of a leak in them
The presence of water in them
The presence of ice at the static port
cards.explain: Fluctuating indications are the sign of water lying in the pipes.

cards.question: An instrument has been changed in the pitot static system. What must be carried out?
options: An approved flushing of the static system
An approved accuracy check of the static ports
An approved leak-proof test
cards.explain: Changing an instrument or a device calls for an approved leak-proof test.

cards.question: What is the purpose of the scale and the feeler-gage used at a static port
options: To assess damage of the aircraft skin against the limits
To check that the static port zone is smooth enough to prevent turbulences
To measure the mouth of the static port against the limits
cards.explain: The scale and feeler-gage are the tools named for assessing skin damage against the AMM limits.

cards.question: Why must the static port zones have a smooth surface
options: So that no turbulences can occur
So that water can drain away from the port
So that no ice can form on the port
cards.explain: A smooth zone keeps the airflow undisturbed so the port senses true static pressure.

cards.question: Where are the limits for damage of the aircraft skin at the static ports found
options: In the ATA chapter for air conditioning or the wiring manual
In the ATA chapter for the aircraft structure or the SRM
In the ATA chapter for the instruments or the IPC
cards.explain: Skin damage is a structural item, so the structure chapter or the SRM holds those limits.

cards.question: What do the results of a leakage depend on
options: The size of the leakage and the altitude of the aircraft
The position of the leakage and the outside air temperature
The size of the leakage and whether the cabin is pressurized
cards.explain: Size of the leak and the pressurization state of the cabin are the two factors given.

cards.question: A static line leaks inside the unpressurized cabin of an aircraft in flight. What does the altimeter do?
options: It slightly increases the indicated altitude
It slightly decreases the indicated altitude
It freezes at the altitude flown when the leak started
cards.explain: The lower cabin pressure reaching the static line reads as a slightly greater altitude.

cards.question: What effect does a static system leakage inside an unpressurized cabin have on the airspeed indicator
options: It shows zero indicated airspeed
It shows a slightly lower indicated airspeed
It shows a slightly higher indicated airspeed
cards.explain: The airspeed indicator reads slightly high, in the same sense as the altimeter.

cards.question: Why do the altimeter and the airspeed indicator decrease their indication when a static line leaks into a pressurized cabin
options: The pressure in the static lines increases
The pressure in the static lines decreases
The pitot and the static pressure become nearly the same
cards.explain: Cabin pressure entering the static lines raises the pressure there, and both instruments read lower as a result.

cards.question: What effect does a static system leakage into a pressurized cabin have on the pressure in the static lines
options: The pressure decreases
The pressure increases
The pressure stays unchanged
cards.explain: Cabin pressure is above the ambient static pressure, so the static lines see a rise.

cards.question: What do the altimeter and the airspeed indicator indicate after a static leakage into a pressurized cabin
options: Both stay unchanged
Both decrease
Both increase
cards.explain: The raised static pressure drives both indications down.

cards.question: A pitot line leaks inside an unpressurized cabin. What does the airspeed indication do?
options: It stays at the value flown when the leak started
It decreases to zero
It increases into the overspeed region
cards.explain: With the pitot line open to the cabin the airspeed indication falls away to zero.

cards.question: Why does the airspeed indication decrease when both the pitot and the static system leak
options: Pitot and static pressure tend to be the same
The total pressure in the pitot line is trapped at a constant value
The static pressure in the lines rises above the pitot pressure
cards.explain: Both lines fill with the same cabin pressure, so the difference the indicator works on shrinks.

cards.question: What effect does a leakage in both the pitot and the static system have on the airspeed indication
options: It is not affected
It decreases
It increases
cards.explain: With both lines open to the same cabin pressure the difference shrinks and the indication falls.

cards.question: Both the pitot system and the static system are leaking. What do the altimeter and the vertical speed indicator show?
options: The same results as for a leakage in the pitot system
The same results as for a leakage in the static system
Correct indications, because the two leaks cancel each other
cards.explain: Those two instruments see only static pressure, so the static leak result still applies.

cards.question: What are the indications with a blocked static system while the aircraft flies at constant altitude and constant airspeed
options: The altitude indication slowly increases
The airspeed indication slowly decreases
There are no changes in the indication
cards.explain: Nothing changes while the trapped static pressure still matches the real one.

cards.question: The static system is blocked and the aircraft climbs. What does the airspeed indicator show?
options: Zero airspeed
A decreasing airspeed indication
An increasing airspeed indication
cards.explain: In the climb the falling total pressure works against a trapped static pressure, so the reading drops.

cards.question: What do the altimeter and the vertical speed indicator indicate with a blocked static system, during a climb and during a descent
options: The same altitude and a vertical speed that follows the aircraft
The same altitude and a vertical speed of zero
A changing altitude and a vertical speed of zero
cards.explain: PDF page 440 prints the frozen altitude and zero vertical speed for the climb and this page the same pair for the descent, since both instruments work from the trapped static pressure.

cards.question: The static system is blocked and the aircraft descends. What does the airspeed indicator show?
options: A decreasing airspeed indication
An increasing airspeed indication
Zero airspeed
cards.explain: In the descent the rising total pressure works against a trapped static pressure, so the reading climbs.

cards.question: Why does the airspeed indicator react like an altimeter when the pitot tube is totally blocked
options: Total and static pressure become nearly equal, so the indication falls away
The static pressure is trapped, so only the changing total pressure moves the indication
The total pressure is trapped, so only the changing static pressure moves the indication
cards.explain: With the total pressure held fixed the indication is driven only by static pressure, which is what an altimeter responds to.

cards.question: What does the airspeed indicator do during a climb with a totally blocked pitot tube
options: It stays at the speed flown when the blockage occurred
It increases and can reach the overspeed region
It decreases and can reach zero
cards.explain: With trapped total pressure and falling static pressure the indication runs up.

cards.question: How does the airspeed indicator behave when the pitot tube is totally blocked
options: It reacts like a vertical speed indicator
It reacts like an altimeter
It reacts like a turn coordinator
cards.explain: Its reading now follows altitude change instead of speed.

cards.question: What does the airspeed indicator do during a descent with a totally blocked pitot tube
options: It remains at the value held during cruise
It increases to a higher indicated airspeed
It decreases to a lower indicated airspeed
cards.explain: The rising static pressure against a trapped total pressure drives the reading down.

cards.question: What happens to the pitot pressure when the pitot tube inlet is blocked but the water drain hole is still open
options: It stays at the value it had before the blockage
It decreases to the value of the static pressure
It increases to the value of the total pressure
cards.explain: The open drain lets the trapped pressure bleed down to static.

cards.question: Why are the altimeter and the vertical speed indicator not affected by a blocked pitot inlet
options: They get both pitot and static pressure
They only get pitot pressure
They only get static pressure
cards.explain: Both instruments are fed from the static system alone.

cards.question: Why can water be present in the pressure pipes
options: They are not drained on a regular basis
They are capped for protection during testing
Their test fittings are used to simulate altitude and speed
cards.explain: The pipes are not drained routinely, so water can collect in them.

cards.question: The static ports of a cold aeroplane are capped and the aircraft is moved into a warm hangar. What happens in the static system?
options: The pressure stays the same
The pressure decreases
The pressure increases
cards.explain: Warming the trapped air in a sealed static system raises its pressure.

cards.question: What happens to the ram pressure when both the pitot inlet and the drain are iced over
options: It is always zero
It is constant at every altitude
It depends on the altitude
cards.explain: With the total pressure held fixed, only the static pressure varies, so ram pressure follows altitude.

cards.question: A device is replaced in lines with screw connections whose connectors are designated red. Which system is concerned and what action is required afterwards
options: The static system, and an approved leak-proof test must be carried out
The pitot system, and the self-sealing connections make a test unnecessary
The pitot system, and an approved leak-proof test must be carried out
cards.explain: Red designates the pitot connections, and changing an instrument or a device calls for an approved leak-proof test.

cards.question: A line was parted only at a quick-disconnect. What applies to the leak-proof test?
options: It is required, as after any other parting
It is required, but only on the static side
It is not required in this case
cards.explain: A parting at a quick-disconnect is the one exception to the leak-proof test requirement.

cards.question: A technician must check the mouth of a static port and also damage to the skin around it. Where are the two sets of limits found?
options: The port mouth limits in the structure chapter or the SRM and the skin damage limits in ATA chapter 34
Both the port mouth limits and the skin damage limits in ATA chapter 34
The port mouth limits in ATA chapter 34 and the skin damage limits in the structure chapter or the SRM
cards.explain: The mouth of the port is covered by ATA chapter 34, while skin damage is covered by the structure chapter or the SRM.

cards.question: A static line breaks inside an unpressurized cabin during flight. How does the vertical speed indicator behave?
options: It jumps once and then shows correct data
It jumps once and then stays at zero
It slowly drifts into a permanent climb indication
cards.explain: The VSI reacts only to the sudden change and then works normally again.

cards.question: The same static line leak is considered in an unpressurized aircraft and in a pressurized one. How does the altimeter behave in each case?
options: It slightly increases the indication in both aircraft
It slightly increases the indication in the unpressurized aircraft and decreases it in the pressurized one
It decreases the indication in the unpressurized aircraft and slightly increases it in the pressurized one
cards.explain: On PDF page 432 the leak into an unpressurized cabin lowers the pressure in the lines, so the altimeter reads slightly higher; on this page the cabin pressure raises the line pressure, so it reads lower.

cards.question: How does the vertical speed indicator behave after a static system leakage in an unpressurized cabin compared with a pressurized cabin
options: A small jump and then correct data in the unpressurized cabin, and an indication depending on cabin rate in the pressurized cabin
An indication depending on cabin rate in the unpressurized cabin, and a small jump and then correct data in the pressurized cabin
A small jump and then correct data in both cabins
cards.explain: On PDF page 432 the unpressurized case gives a single small jump and then correct data; on this page the pressurized cabin makes the indication follow the cabin rate.

cards.question: A static line leaks into a pressurized cabin. What does the vertical speed indication now depend on?
options: The cabin rate
The aircraft rate of climb
The size of the leak
cards.explain: With cabin air in the static line the VSI follows the cabin rate, not the aircraft.

cards.question: A pitot line is leaking inside the cabin. How does the airspeed indication behave in an unpressurized aircraft compared with a pressurized one?
options: It decreases to zero in the unpressurized aircraft and is unpredictable in the pressurized one
It decreases to zero in both aircraft
It is unpredictable in the unpressurized aircraft and decreases to zero in the pressurized one
cards.explain: With no cabin pressure the two pressures equalise and the indication falls to zero, while cabin pressure makes the result depend on altitude and cabin pressure.

cards.question: Why does the airspeed indication fall to zero with a pitot leakage in an unpressurized cabin
options: The pitot pressure rises with the cabin pressure
Static and pitot pressure become nearly the same
The static pressure becomes much greater than the pitot pressure
cards.explain: The airspeed indicator works on the difference between the two pressures, which is now almost nil.

cards.question: A pitot line leaks inside a pressurized cabin. What can be said about the airspeed indication?
options: It always falls to zero, because pitot and static pressure become equal
It is unpredictable, because it depends on altitude and cabin pressure
It always rises, because the cabin pressure is higher than the static pressure
cards.explain: With a pressurized cabin the two varying pressures make the indication unpredictable.

cards.question: Which instruments are disturbed by a leakage in the pitot system alone compared with a leakage in both the pitot and the static system
options: The airspeed indicator and the altimeter, compared with the airspeed indicator and the vertical speed indication
The airspeed indicator and the vertical speed indication, compared with the airspeed indicator alone
The airspeed indicator alone, compared with the airspeed indicator, the altimeter and the vertical speed indication
cards.explain: PDF page 436 prints that a pitot leak affects the airspeed indicator only, and this page adds the altimeter and the vertical speed indication once the static system leaks as well.

cards.question: Both the pitot system and the static system leak inside an unpressurized cabin. What does the altimeter do?
options: It slightly increases the indicated altitude
It holds the altitude it had when the leakage started
It slightly decreases the indicated altitude
cards.explain: This page refers the altimeter back to the static leakage result, and PDF page 432 prints that result for an unpressurized cabin as a slightly increased indicated altitude.

cards.question: An aircraft cruises at constant altitude and constant airspeed with a blocked static system and then begins a climb. What does the altimeter do?
options: It continues to display the same altitude
It jumps once and then follows the climb correctly
It begins to increase its indication as the climb starts
cards.explain: The trapped static pressure cannot change, so the altimeter holds the same altitude in level flight and through the climb.

cards.question: Why does the airspeed indication decrease during a climb with a blocked static system
options: The total pressure from the pitot tube decreases while the trapped static pressure stays constant
The total pressure and the static pressure both decrease together
The total pressure from the pitot tube stays constant while the static pressure decreases
cards.explain: Only the total pressure falls; the blocked static side cannot follow it.

cards.question: How does the airspeed indication with a blocked static system during a climb compare with a descent
options: Decreasing during both the climb and the descent
Decreasing during the climb and increasing during the descent
Increasing during the climb and decreasing during the descent
cards.explain: PDF page 440 prints the decreasing indication in the climb and this page the increasing one in the descent, because the trapped static pressure stays fixed while the total pressure falls and then rises.

cards.question: Why does the airspeed indication increase during a descent with a blocked static system
options: The total pressure and the static pressure both increase together
The total pressure from the pitot tube increases while the trapped static pressure remains constant
The trapped static pressure increases while the total pressure remains constant
cards.explain: Only the total pressure rises; the blocked static side stays where it was.

cards.question: Two aircraft climb, one with a blocked static system and one with a completely blocked pitot tube. What does the airspeed indicator show in each?
options: A decreasing indication with the blocked static system and an increasing indication with the blocked pitot tube
An increasing indication with the blocked static system and a decreasing indication with the blocked pitot tube
A decreasing indication in both aircraft
cards.explain: PDF page 440 prints the decreasing indication with the static side blocked, while this page prints the increasing one with the pitot side blocked, because the falling static pressure then drives the instrument.

cards.question: How does the airspeed indication during a descent with a blocked static system compare with a completely blocked pitot tube
options: Decreasing with the blocked static system and increasing with the blocked pitot tube
Increasing with both blockages
Increasing with the blocked static system and decreasing with the blocked pitot tube
cards.explain: PDF page 442 prints the increasing indication with the static side blocked, while this page prints the decreasing one with the pitot side blocked, because the rising static pressure then drives the instrument.

cards.question: The pitot tube becomes totally blocked in cruise and the thrust is then increased to accelerate. What does the airspeed indicator show?
options: A rise in the indicated speed
No change in the indicated speed
A fall of the indicated speed to zero
cards.explain: At constant altitude neither pressure changes, so the reading is frozen whatever the thrust.

cards.question: The pitot inlet of an aircraft is found blocked by ice. Which indication shows that the water drain hole is still open?
options: The airspeed indication stops responding to changes of thrust
The airspeed indication decreases to zero
The airspeed indication increases into the overspeed region
cards.explain: With the drain open the pitot pressure falls to static and the indication drops to zero, which a completely blocked tube does not do.

cards.question: What happens to the pitot pressure and the airspeed indication when the pitot inlet is iced over but the drain is free
options: The pitot pressure falls to static pressure and the airspeed indication increases
The pitot pressure remains constant and the airspeed indication decreases to zero
The pitot pressure falls to static pressure and the airspeed indication decreases to zero
cards.explain: The open drain lets the pitot pressure fall to static pressure, leaving no difference for the indicator to show.

cards.question: Two pitot probes are examined, one iced at the inlet only and one iced at the inlet and the drain. What does each condition say about the heating?
options: Insufficient heating for the inlet only, and defective or deactivated heating when both are iced
Defective or deactivated heating for the inlet only, and insufficient heating when both are iced
Insufficient heating in both conditions
cards.explain: Ice at the inlet alone points to heating that is too weak, while ice at both openings points to heating that is defective or switched off.

cards.question: The pitot inlet is iced over but the drain is free. What does this tell you about the heating?
options: The heating is insufficient
The heating is working correctly
The heating is defective or deactivated
cards.explain: Ice only at the inlet points to heating that is working but not enough.

cards.question: Both the pitot inlet and the drain are iced over. What does this say about the heating and the pitot pressure?
options: The heating is defective or deactivated and the pitot pressure falls to static pressure
The heating is defective or deactivated and the pitot pressure remains constant
The heating is insufficient and the pitot pressure falls to static pressure
cards.explain: Complete icing means the heating has failed or is off, and the sealed pitot pressure cannot change.

cards.question: What is measured in the barometric method of determining altitude
options: Satellite signal delay
Radio wave delay
Air pressure
cards.explain: The barometer method measures air pressure; the other two quantities belong to the radio altimeter and to GPS.

cards.question: A barometric altimeter is connected to one pneumatic line only. Which pressure does it measure?
options: Pitot pressure
Total pressure
Static pressure
cards.explain: The barometric altimeter is an aneroid barometer working on static pressure only.

cards.question: What is the shape of the ISA pressure graph at low altitudes
options: Strongly exponential
A series of steps
Nearly linear
cards.explain: Close to the ground the pressure against altitude curve is nearly a straight line.

cards.question: Which pressure decrease corresponds to an altitude increase of 30 ft at low altitude
options: 10 hPa
1 hPa
30 hPa
cards.explain: The printed relationship at low altitude is 30 ft per 1 hPa.

cards.question: What does the baro set knob give the altimeter
options: A new reference pressure
A new static pressure source
A new scale calibration in metres
cards.explain: The knob only changes the reference pressure the indication is based on.

cards.question: The crew is preparing for departure. Which pressure do they set on the altimeters?
options: The actual pressure at ground level
The actual pressure related to sea level
The standard pressure of the ISA
cards.explain: Before takeoff the reference is the actual sea level pressure, which is the QNH setting.

cards.question: What name is given to the reference pressure used for QNE
options: Standard
Ambient
Nautical
cards.explain: The 1013 hPa reference is called standard.

cards.question: Who may select the barometric correction on an altimeter, besides the pilots
options: The air data computer
Air traffic control
Maintenance personnel
cards.explain: The manual names pilots and maintenance personnel as the ones who select the baro correction.

cards.question: How does a barometer determine altitude
options: By using the increase in pressure with increasing altitude
By using the delay of a reflected radio wave
By using the decrease in pressure with increasing altitude
cards.explain: Pressure falls as altitude rises, and the barometer uses that relationship.

cards.question: A method of determining altitude uses the WGS84 gravitation model as its reference instead of the ground. Which method is it?
options: Barometer
GPS
Radio altimeter
cards.explain: WGS84 is the reference of the GPS method; the barometer uses pressure and the radio altimeter uses the ground.

cards.question: How is the interior of a barometric altimeter casing connected
options: To the outside air via the static system
To a sealed reference vacuum
To the outside air via the pitot system
cards.explain: Outside air reaches the inside of the case through the static system.

cards.question: An aircraft climbs. What happens inside its barometric altimeter?
options: Pressure decreases, the bellows contract and the pointer rises
Pressure increases, the bellows expand and the pointer falls
Pressure decreases, the bellows expand and the pointer rises
cards.explain: Falling pressure around the capsule lets the bellows expand, which drives the pointer up the scale.

cards.question: Which construction feature distinguishes an encoding altimeter
options: An additional static port and a drum
Additional bellows and electrical connectors
Additional pointers and a second baro scale
cards.explain: The encoding altimeter carries extra bellows and electrical connectors on top of the normal altimeter.

cards.question: An encoding altimeter puts out an ALT signal. Which system receives it?
options: The air data computer
The ATC transponder system
The static system
cards.explain: The encoding altimeter feeds the ALT signal to the ATC transponder.

cards.question: Why is an encoding altimeter connected to the ATC transponder system?
options: So that the transponder can set the baro correction of the altimeter
So that ground control can be informed about the altitude of the aircraft
So that the crew can be informed about the ground pressure
cards.explain: The purpose of the ALT signal is to pass the aircraft altitude to ground control.

cards.question: In which aircraft are encoding altimeters found
options: Some small aircraft
All aircraft fitted with an air data computer
Only aircraft without a transponder
cards.explain: The encoding altimeter is described as a fit found in some small aircraft.

cards.question: Why is an encoding altimeter fitted with electrical connectors
options: To provide the ALT signal for the ATC transponder system
To drive the additional bellows inside the instrument
To receive the reference pressure from an air data computer
cards.explain: The electrical connectors carry the ALT signal that the ATC transponder system needs.

cards.question: How does the baro set knob work in a pneumatic indicator
options: It moves the bellows stack alone
It directly turns the whole altimeter mechanism
It sends a correction signal to the air data computer
cards.explain: In a pneumatic instrument the setting is made mechanically by turning the whole mechanism.

cards.question: A new reference pressure is selected on an electrical altitude indicator. How is the correction made?
options: Electrically inside the indicator or via an air data computer
Pneumatically, by an additional set of bellows
Mechanically, by turning the whole altimeter mechanism
cards.explain: Electrical indicators have no mechanism to turn, so the correction is done electrically.

cards.question: An airport lies well above sea level and the altimeter is set to QNH. What does the instrument show on the ground?
options: The height of the aircraft above the runway
Zero feet
The altitude of the airport related to mean sea level
cards.explain: With sea level as the reference, an airport above sea level indicates its own elevation.

cards.question: The aircraft is descending and reaches the Transition Level. What do the pilots do with the altimeters?
options: They adjust them to 1013 hPa
They adjust them to the pressure used at the departure airport
They adjust them to the actual pressure at the destination airport
cards.explain: At the Transition Level the standard setting is replaced by the destination setting.

cards.question: How is a new reference pressure applied in a pneumatic altimeter compared with an electrical indicator
options: By turning the whole altimeter mechanism, compared with a correction made electrically inside the indicator or via an air data computer
By turning the whole altimeter mechanism, in the pneumatic indicator and in the electrical indicator alike
By a correction made electrically inside the indicator or via an air data computer, compared with turning the whole altimeter mechanism
cards.explain: The pneumatic instrument is re-referenced mechanically, the electrical one electrically inside itself or through an air data computer.

cards.question: Which baro correction makes the altimeter read zero on the ground
options: QNH
QNE
QFE
cards.explain: QFE uses the ambient pressure at ground level, so the indication on the ground is zero.

cards.question: To which level is the pressure used for QFE related
options: Ground level
The standard atmosphere
Mean sea level
cards.explain: QFE is the ambient pressure at ground level, unlike QNH which is related to mean sea level.

cards.question: An aircraft is in flight with QFE set on its altimeter. What does the indication represent?
options: The height above mean sea level
The altitude in the standard atmosphere
The height above the ground
cards.explain: With the ground as reference the instrument shows height above the ground.

cards.question: Why do pilots of medium and large aircraft normally not use QFE?
options: Their baro scales cannot be set that low
The QFE value is not transmitted by data link
They can use a radio altimeter system
cards.explain: A radio altimeter already gives the height above the ground, so the QFE setting is not needed.

cards.question: An aircraft in flight has the baro correction for QNH set. What does the altimeter read?
options: The height above mean sea level
The height above the ground
The height above the transition altitude
cards.explain: QNH refers everything to mean sea level, in flight as well as on the ground.

cards.question: A technician selects QNE on an altimeter. Which reference is then used?
options: The ambient pressure at mean sea level on the day
The ambient pressure at the airport
The standard atmosphere with 1013 hPa
cards.explain: QNE is always the fixed standard atmosphere value, not a value measured on the day.

cards.question: Where is the QNE setting normally used
options: On the ground, not in flight
During takeoff and landing only
In flight, not on the ground
cards.explain: QNE is the in-flight setting; on the ground the airport settings are used.

cards.question: What is the advantage of QNE
options: All aircraft in cruise flight use the same reference pressure
The altimeter reads zero at touchdown
Every aircraft reads its own height above the ground
cards.explain: The whole point of QNE is a single common reference for all aircraft in the cruise.

cards.question: What does an altimeter in flight indicate with the baro correction for QFE compared with QNH
options: The height above the ground with both corrections
The height above the ground with QFE and the height above mean sea level with QNH
The height above mean sea level with QFE and the height above the ground with QNH
cards.explain: QFE refers the indication to the ground and QNH to mean sea level.

cards.question: An altimeter set to QFE indicates 0 ft at touchdown because of which reference
options: Its reference is the standard atmosphere with 1013 hPa
Its reference is the actual pressure related on ground level
Its reference is the actual pressure related on mean sea level
cards.explain: QFE takes the pressure at ground level as its reference, so the indication is zero on the ground.

cards.question: An altimeter is set to standard pressure. Under which condition is its indicated altitude equal to the true altitude?
options: When the pressure at sea level is really 1013 hPa
When the airport elevation is zero
When the aircraft is above the transition altitude
cards.explain: The conversion from static pressure to altitude only matches the true altitude when the real sea level pressure is the calibration value.

cards.question: A crew keeps 1013 hPa set on the altimeters for the whole cruise. Why does the indication not give the true altitude everywhere along the route?
options: Because the indication is only correct where the pressure at sea level really is 1013 hPa
Because the pressure graph of the standard atmosphere is only linear at low altitudes
Because all aircraft in cruise flight select a different reference pressure
cards.explain: Indicated altitude only equals true altitude where the real sea level pressure is 1013 hPa, and PDF page 464 adds that the altimeters cannot be reset for every point of the route.

cards.question: Why do all aircraft in cruise use one common selected pressure instead of the local pressure?
options: So that they all keep the same altitude separation in low and high pressure areas
So that ground control can read the elevation of the airports
So that each of them indicates its true height above the ground
cards.explain: A common reference keeps the vertical separation between aircraft consistent whatever the local pressure is.

cards.question: An altimeter is left calibrated to 1013 hPa while the real pressure at sea level below the aircraft is lower. What will the instrument indicate?
options: The correct altitude
Too high an altitude
Too low an altitude
cards.explain: With the reference set higher than the real sea level pressure, the instrument over-reads.

cards.question: An aircraft passes the Transition Altitude after takeoff and later the Transition Level before landing. Which setting is made at each point?
options: 1013 hPa at both the Transition Altitude and the Transition Level
The actual pressure at the departure airport at the Transition Altitude and 1013 hPa at the Transition Level
1013 hPa at the Transition Altitude and the actual pressure at the destination airport at the Transition Level
cards.explain: The common standard pressure is taken at the Transition Altitude on the way up and given back for the local pressure at the Transition Level on the way down.

cards.question: Two altimeters at the same airport, which lies above sea level, read differently on the ground, one showing zero and the other the elevation of the airport. Which baro corrections are set?
options: QFE on the one showing zero and QNE on the one showing the elevation
QNH on the one showing zero and QFE on the one showing the elevation
QFE on the one showing zero and QNH on the one showing the elevation
cards.explain: QFE is referenced to the ground and reads zero there, while QNH is referenced to mean sea level and shows the airport elevation.

cards.question: The QNE and the QNH altimeter calibration both refer the altitude to mean sea level. What is the difference between them
options: QNE uses the actual pressure related to ground level while QNH uses the standard atmosphere with 1013 hPa
QNE uses the actual pressure related to mean sea level while QNH uses the standard atmosphere with 1013 hPa
QNE uses the standard atmosphere with 1013 hPa while QNH uses the actual pressure related to mean sea level
cards.explain: Both refer the altitude to mean sea level, but QNE always takes the standard pressure while QNH takes the actual one.

cards.question: Which type of measuring instrument is the airspeed indicator
options: A differential pressure meter
An absolute pressure meter
A differential temperature meter
cards.explain: The instrument works on the difference between two pressures, so it is a differential pressure meter.

cards.question: In which unit is the scale of the airspeed indicator calibrated
options: Kilometres per hour
Knots
Nautical miles
cards.explain: The printed text gives knots as the unit of the scale.

cards.question: What does the green band on the airspeed indicator of a small aircraft show
options: Normal Operating Range
Full Flap Operating Range
Caution range
cards.explain: Green marks the normal operating range on the scale.

cards.question: What does the white band on the airspeed indicator of a small aircraft show
options: Caution range
Full Flap Operating Range
Normal Operating Range
cards.explain: White marks the range in which the flaps may be fully used.

cards.question: What does the red mark on a helicopter airspeed indicator show
options: The speed that must never be exceeded
The range of transition lift
The maximum speed allowed for autorotation
cards.explain: Red marks VNE, the never exceed speed.

cards.question: What does the red-white mark on a helicopter airspeed indicator show
options: The maximum speed allowed for autorotation under all conditions
The speed that must never be exceeded
The range of transition lift
cards.explain: The red-white mark is the autorotation speed limit.

cards.question: Where does the aircraft move at the speed called true airspeed
options: Relative to the airspeed indicator scale
Through the surrounding air
Over the ground
cards.explain: TAS is defined as the aircraft speed through the surrounding air mass.

cards.question: What is the speed shown on the indicator called
options: Indicated airspeed
Ground speed
True airspeed
cards.explain: What the instrument displays is the indicated airspeed.

cards.question: A technician traces the pitot line to the airspeed indicator capsule. Which pressure does that line deliver to the capsule interior?
options: Total pressure from the pitot system
Static pressure from the static system
Dynamic pressure from the static system
cards.explain: The capsule interior receives total pressure, which the pitot system delivers.

cards.question: The capsule of an airspeed indicator sits inside a sealed casing. Which pressure acts inside that casing?
options: Dynamic pressure from the pitot system
Total pressure from the pitot system
Static pressure from the static system
cards.explain: The casing is fed from the static system, so static pressure surrounds the capsule.

cards.question: In an airspeed indicator, what does the difference between total pressure and static pressure give
options: Total pressure
Dynamic pressure
Static pressure
cards.explain: Total pressure minus static pressure is by definition the dynamic pressure.

cards.question: A technician is asked what the indicated airspeed value is used for. Which answer is correct?
options: As a value for altitude and for the maximum rate of climb
As a value for lift and for the maximum load on the flaps
As a value for thrust and for the maximum cabin pressure
cards.explain: The manual lists lift and maximum load on the flaps and airframe among the uses of the IAS.

cards.question: An aircraft is fitted with a primary flight display instead of a mechanical airspeed indicator. How is airspeed presented?
options: As a speed limit marking on the PFD
As a speed bug on the PFD
As a speed band on the PFD
cards.explain: The third type of airspeed indication listed is the speed band shown on the PFD.

cards.question: How are the airspeed limits shown in small aircraft
options: A digital readout beside the airspeed indicator
A movable pointer driven by the air data computer
Coloured ranges and lines on the airspeed indicator scale
cards.explain: Small aircraft carry the limits as colour markings painted on the instrument scale.

cards.question: An aeroplane is being flown with the airspeed in the yellow band. Which condition applies?
options: It may only be used in smooth air without hard manoeuvres
It may only be used with the flaps extended
It may be used in any air, including hard manoeuvres
cards.explain: The caution range is restricted to smooth air with no hard manoeuvres.

cards.question: The slight increase of VMO with altitude results from taking account of which error
options: The instrument error of the IAS
The compressibility error of the IAS
The static source error of the IAS
cards.explain: The manual attributes the slight rise to the compressibility error of the IAS.

cards.question: A crew wants a minimum speed indication in the cockpit. On which aircraft is it available, and where is it shown?
options: Only on aircraft with a glass cockpit, on the speed tape of the PFD
On all jet aircraft, as a coloured band on the airspeed indicator scale
Only on piston engine aircraft, as a red line on the airspeed indicator
cards.explain: The minimum speed indication is a glass cockpit feature shown on the PFD speed tape.

cards.question: How does the yellow band on the airspeed indicator of a small aircraft differ from the green band
options: It is the caution range, to be used only in smooth air without hard manoeuvres, while the green band is the full flap operating range
It is the caution range, to be used only in smooth air without hard manoeuvres, while the green band is the normal operating range
It is the normal operating range, while the green band is the caution range, to be used only in smooth air without hard manoeuvres
cards.explain: The green band is the normal operating range while the yellow band is a caution range with conditions attached to its use.

cards.question: A helicopter airspeed indicator carries two essential marked limits. What makes them necessary?
options: The engine power limits of the helicopter
The aerodynamic properties of the helicopter
The maximum take-off weight of the helicopter
cards.explain: The manual gives the aerodynamic properties of the helicopter as the reason for the two marked limits.

cards.question: An aircraft is flown at sea level in standard conditions and its IAS equals its TAS. Which further condition must be met?
options: With negligible compressibility error
With negligible instrument error
With negligible static source error
cards.explain: The manual gives two conditions for IAS and TAS to coincide: standard conditions at sea level and negligible static source error.

cards.question: TAS is obtained from IAS by correcting for instrument error, static source error, dynamic pressure error and which further quantity
options: Magnetic variation
Aircraft weight
Air density
cards.explain: Air density is the fourth correction listed for deriving TAS from IAS.

cards.question: A jet aeroplane climbs from low altitude to high altitude. Which limit governs its maximum speed at the higher altitude?
options: The maximum allowed Mach number MMO
The maximum operating velocity VMO
The never exceed speed VNE
cards.explain: Above a certain altitude the Mach limit MMO takes over from the dynamic pressure limit VMO.

cards.question: Why can the speed limit of a jet aeroplane at low altitude be read directly as an indicated airspeed?
options: Because the limit there depends on dynamic pressure, and the indicated airspeed indicator is a dynamic pressure indicator
Because the limit there depends on dynamic pressure, and the indicated airspeed indicator is a total pressure indicator
Because the limit there depends on the speed of sound, and the indicated airspeed indicator is a dynamic pressure indicator
cards.explain: This page prints that the low altitude limit is a dynamic pressure limit, and PDF page 468 prints that the indicated airspeed is a dynamic pressure indicator, so the limit can be marked as a speed.

cards.question: How do VMO and MMO change as a jet aeroplane climbs
options: VMO decreases while MMO stays constant or increases slightly
VMO stays constant or increases slightly while MMO decreases
VMO and MMO both decrease
cards.explain: VMO holds or rises a little with altitude while MMO falls, because the speed of sound falls.

cards.question: A helicopter airspeed indicator carries a red mark and a red-white mark. Which limit does each of them give?
options: The red mark the speed that must never be exceeded, the red-white mark the maximum speed allowed for autorotation
The red mark the speed that must never be exceeded, the red-white mark the range of transition lift
The red mark the maximum speed allowed for autorotation, the red-white mark the speed that must never be exceeded
cards.explain: The plain red mark is the never exceed speed and the red-white mark is the autorotation limit.

cards.question: An aircraft climbs while holding a constant indicated airspeed. What happens to the difference between IAS and TAS?
options: It decreases, because the air density decreases
It increases, because the air density decreases
It stays the same, because the IAS is corrected for density
cards.explain: Falling air density with altitude widens the gap between IAS and TAS.

cards.question: An aircraft is flown at sea level in standard conditions, but its static source error is not negligible. Do the indicated airspeed and the true airspeed coincide?
options: No, because they coincide only when the static source error is negligible as well
Yes, because at sea level the two speeds always coincide
Yes, because the static source error only separates them at altitude
cards.explain: The printed condition is both standard conditions at sea level and a negligible static source error, so failing one of them is enough to separate the two speeds.

cards.question: An aircraft is not fitted with an air data computer. What must be provided instead?
options: A second airspeed indicator for comparison
Correction tables in the Flight Operations Manual
Correction tables in the aircraft technical log
cards.explain: Without an air data computer the corrections come from tables in the Flight Operations Manual.

cards.question: What is the purpose of the mach meter
options: To enable flight at the never exceed speed and with maximum rate of climb
To enable flight at the maximum operating velocity and with minimum structural load
To enable flight at the maximum operating mach number and with economic efficiency
cards.explain: The manual gives exactly these two purposes for the mach meter.

cards.question: A technician opens a mach meter on the bench. Which two sensing elements are inside it?
options: Aneroid bellows and a capillary restrictor
Differential pressure bellows and a bimetallic element
Differential pressure bellows and aneroid bellows
cards.explain: The manual lists these two elements as the contents of a mach meter.

cards.question: The mach number M is defined as the relation of which two speeds
options: Speed flown to speed of sound
Speed of sound to speed flown
True airspeed to calibrated airspeed
cards.explain: Mach number is speed flown divided by speed of sound.

cards.question: Which errors is the indicated mach number Mi subject to
options: Instrument error and static source error
Static source error and density error
Instrument error and compressibility error
cards.explain: These are the two errors stated for Mi.

cards.question: In a jet aircraft, how is the speed limit shown in the airspeed indicator
options: A red and white VMO / MMO pointer
A red and white VNE pointer
A red and green VMO / MMO pointer
cards.explain: The manual names the red and white VMO / MMO pointer.

cards.question: On the speed tape of a PFD, how is the speed limit shown
options: An amber and black area
A red and black area
A red and white area
cards.explain: The PFD speed tape uses a red and black area.

cards.question: What does the variometer measure in order to display vertical speed
options: Vertical acceleration forces
Air pressure changes
Air temperature changes
cards.explain: The variometer works from changes in air pressure.

cards.question: In which units is the variometer scale calibrated
options: Knots or m/sec
Ft/min or m/sec
Ft/sec or m/min
cards.explain: The manual gives ft/min or m/sec.

cards.question: What does the abbreviation IVSI stand for
options: Instantaneous Vertical Speed Indicator
Integrated Vertical Speed Indicator
Inertial Vertical Speed Indicator
cards.explain: IVSI is the instantaneous vertical speed indicator, giving undelayed indication.

cards.question: What does the IVSI indicator use to produce its undelayed indication
options: A small fan with a spring loaded vane
A small pump with a magnetically held piston
A small pump with a spring loaded piston
cards.explain: The manual describes a small pump with a spring loaded piston.

cards.question: A diaphragm variometer is stripped for overhaul. What seals the air gap?
options: A felt washer
Badger hair
A rubber lip seal
cards.explain: The manual states the gap is sealed with badger hair.

cards.question: What sets the central position of a diaphragm variometer
options: A permanent magnet
A coiled spring
A hairspring driven by the capillary
cards.explain: A coiled spring sets the central position.

cards.question: Why is a mach indication needed for flight at high altitude
options: Because the limit there is the maximum operating velocity and dynamic pressure is a function of altitude
Because the limit there is the maximum operating mach number and the speed of sound is a function of dynamic pressure
Because the limit there is the maximum operating mach number and the speed of sound is a function of altitude
cards.explain: PDF page 470 prints that at higher altitudes the limit is the maximum operating mach number, and this page prints that the speed of sound is a function of altitude, so the limit cannot be read from an airspeed alone.

cards.question: What does the shock formation caused by compression of the air do to the airflow and the forces on the aircraft
options: It prevents turbulent airflow, decreases drag and increases lift
It prevents laminar airflow, increases drag and decreases lift
It prevents laminar airflow, decreases drag and decreases lift
cards.explain: The page states shock formation stops laminar flow, raises drag and lowers lift.

cards.question: Why can the speed of sound be represented as a function of altitude
options: Because it is a function of temperature, and under standard conditions temperature is a function of altitude
Because it is a function of density, and under standard conditions density is a function of airspeed
Because it is a function of static pressure, and under standard conditions pressure is a function of temperature
cards.explain: The chain given is speed of sound to temperature to altitude.

cards.question: The MMO marking on a stand-alone mach meter is the adjustable version and has to be re-set. Where is this carried out?
options: On the ramp before each flight
In the workshop
In the cockpit by the pilot
cards.explain: The manual calls adjusting the MMO marking a workshop task.

cards.question: How is the indicated mach number Mi obtained compared with the true mach number MT
options: Mi is calculated from pitot pressure and dynamic pressure while MT is calculated from the speed of sound and the outside temperature
Mi is calculated by the air data computer while MT is calculated from pitot pressure and dynamic pressure
Mi is calculated from pitot pressure and dynamic pressure while MT is calculated by the air data computer
cards.explain: Mi comes from the pressures at the instrument while MT is worked out by the air data computer.

cards.question: From which pressures is the indicated mach number Mi calculated
options: Pitot pressure and accumulator pressure
Dynamic pressure and cabin pressure
Pitot pressure and dynamic pressure
cards.explain: The manual names pitot pressure and dynamic pressure as the inputs for Mi.

cards.question: Which computer calculates the true mach number MT
options: The flight management computer
The central maintenance computer
The air data computer
cards.explain: The manual states the air data computer calculates MT.

cards.question: Two mach values are available on an aircraft, one free of instrument and static source error. Which value is that?
options: The maximum operating mach number MMO
The true mach number MT
The indicated mach number Mi
cards.explain: MT is defined as being without instrument and static source error, unlike Mi.

cards.question: Why do jet aircraft need a pointer or speed tape marking to show the maximum allowed airspeed
options: Because the speed limit is a fixed value as the VNE is in piston engine aircraft
Because the speed limit is not a fixed value as the VNE is in piston engine aircraft
Because the airspeed indicator cannot show indicated airspeed above the speed of sound
cards.explain: The limit varies, so it must be displayed, unlike a fixed VNE.

cards.question: How does VMO behave with increasing altitude when the compressibility error of the IAS is taken into account
options: It always decreases in the same way as MMO
It is either constant or it increases slightly
It is either constant or it decreases slightly
cards.explain: The manual states VMO is constant or rises slightly with altitude.

cards.question: An aircraft climbs steadily and the MMO limit falls. Why does it fall?
options: Because the speed of sound decreases
Because the compressibility error increases
Because the dynamic pressure decreases
cards.explain: The falling speed of sound is the stated reason.

cards.question: Why do all jet aircraft have an independent aural overspeed warning
options: Because of the danger of aircraft damage during an overspeed
Because the static source error becomes too large at high altitude
Because the airspeed indicator is unreadable at high mach numbers
cards.explain: The stated reason is the risk of damaging the aircraft.

cards.question: What does the mach - airspeed warning switch contain
options: The same aneroid capsule stack as an altimeter
The same capillary tube as a variometer
The same bellows as a mach meter
cards.explain: The switch uses mach meter bellows.

cards.question: How is the aural overspeed warning produced
options: From the cockpit loudspeakers triggered by the master warning system, or by a separate system with a horn from the stall warning
From the cockpit loudspeakers triggered by the air data computer, or by a separate system with a clacker sound
From the cockpit loudspeakers triggered by the master warning system, or by a separate system with a clacker sound
cards.explain: These are the two arrangements given for the aural warning.

cards.question: Why is a vertical speed indicator connected to the static system only
options: Because it works from the difference between total pressure and static pressure
Because it works from changes of static pressure acting on its bellows
Because it works from the delay of the total pressure through a capillary
cards.explain: The instrument senses air pressure changes with static pressure on both sides of its bellows, so it needs no pitot connection.

cards.question: Why is the outside of the variometer bellows fed through a capillary
options: So that the same pressure always acts inside and outside the bellows
So that the pressure change inside the bellows is delayed
So that the pressure change outside the bellows is delayed
cards.explain: The capillary holds back the pressure change on the outside, which is what creates the difference the pointer shows.

cards.question: How are the two sides of the differential pressure bellows of a mechanical variometer supplied
options: The inside directly with total pressure, the outside delayed via a capillary
The inside directly with static pressure, the outside delayed via a capillary
The outside directly with static pressure, the inside delayed via a capillary
cards.explain: Static pressure reaches the inside directly and the outside through the capillary.

cards.question: An aircraft holds a constant altitude so static pressure stays constant. What does the mechanical variometer show?
options: Zero, because the same pressure acts inside and outside the bellows
A small climb, because the capillary keeps the outside pressure higher
A small descent, because the bellows remain partly compressed
cards.explain: With equal pressures either side of the bellows the pointer reads zero.

cards.question: An aircraft with an IVSI enters and leaves a turn with a high bank angle. What should be expected?
options: A total loss of indication, because the piston is locked by the acceleration
A correct vertical speed indication, because the piston compensates for bank angle
An inaccurate vertical speed indication, because any vertical acceleration affects the piston
cards.explain: Any vertical acceleration acts on the piston, so turn entry and exit give a wrong reading.

cards.question: What produces the force that moves the diaphragm and the pointer of a diaphragm variometer
options: The difference between static pressure and accumulator pressure
The difference between accumulator pressure and cabin pressure
The difference between static pressure and total pressure
cards.explain: The driving difference is between static and accumulator pressure.

cards.question: How is pressure balanced out in a diaphragm variometer
options: Via a calibrated orifice in the centre of the diaphragm
Via the air gap between the diaphragm and the casing
Via a capillary tube between the diaphragm and the casing
cards.explain: Balancing takes place through the air gap between diaphragm and casing.

cards.question: A precision variometer is required for a glider. Why is the diaphragm type chosen?
options: Because diaphragm variometers need no static source
Because diaphragm variometers are exact
Because diaphragm variometers have the longest time constant
cards.explain: Their accuracy is the stated reason for their use as precision instruments.

cards.question: A machmeter is opened and found to contain a differential pressure bellows and an aneroid bellows. Which instruments use these same two sensing elements?
options: The airspeed indicator uses a differential pressure capsule and the vertical speed indicator an aneroid capsule
The airspeed indicator uses a differential pressure capsule and the altimeter an aneroid capsule
The altimeter uses a differential pressure capsule and the airspeed indicator an aneroid capsule
cards.explain: PDF page 468 prints that the airspeed indicator has a differential pressure capsule and PDF page 454 that the altimeter's measuring component is an aneroid capsule, which are the two bellows listed here.

cards.question: A jet aeroplane in high altitude cruise triggers its overspeed warning. Which limit has been exceeded, and does the warning depend on the airspeed indication?
options: MMO, and the detection is independent of the airspeed indication
VMO, and the detection is independent of the airspeed indication
MMO, and the detection is taken from the airspeed indication
cards.explain: PDF page 470 prints that at higher altitudes the limit is the maximum allowed mach number, and this page prints that the overspeed detection is always independent of the airspeed indication.

cards.question: The airspeed indication in the cockpit has failed. What does this mean for overspeed detection?
options: Detection continues, because it is always independent of the airspeed indication
Detection continues only while the aircraft is below the tropopause
Detection is lost, because it is taken from the airspeed indication
cards.explain: Detection is stated to be always independent of the airspeed indication.

cards.question: Why is the pointer movement of a mechanical variometer delayed when the vertical speed changes
options: Because the change is immediate inside the bellows but delayed outside by capillary action and the larger volume
Because the change is immediate outside the bellows but delayed inside by capillary action and the larger volume
Because the pointer linkage is deliberately damped by a friction brake
cards.explain: The capillary and the larger outer volume delay the outside pressure change.

cards.question: How does a mechanical variometer respond to a change of vertical speed compared with an instantaneous vertical speed indicator
options: Delayed in both, because both feed the outside of the bellows through a capillary
Undelayed in the mechanical variometer, and delayed in the IVSI because an acceleration piston is installed
Delayed in the mechanical variometer, and undelayed in the IVSI because an acceleration piston is installed
cards.explain: PDF page 486 prints that the pointer movement is delayed on a change of vertical speed, and this page prints that the IVSI removes that delay with an acceleration piston.

cards.question: An aircraft begins a descent. How does the IVSI piston give an immediate indication?
options: The negative gravity force closes the capillary so that the outside static pressure changes first
The negative gravity force moves the piston up and raises the pressure inside the bellows before the outside static pressure changes
The negative gravity force moves the piston down and lowers the pressure inside the bellows before the outside static pressure changes
cards.explain: The piston raises bellows pressure ahead of the real static pressure change.
